questions.title: WI:SG-1.Q1
questions.text: Does the organization implement the following methods of segmentation? (Select all that apply)
questions.supplemental:
Importance: Network segmentation contains adversary activities and non-adversarial stresses (e.g., fires, floods) to the enclave, system segment, or facility in which they have established a presence and limits the set of possible targets to which malware can be easily propagated. This question addresses the different types of network segmentation that can be applied to achieve this goal.

Question Intent: Determine if the organization has developed and executed a network segmentation strategy commensurate with the sensitivity levels of its systems and data. Evaluate both “vertical” and “horizontal” or “lateral” segmentation.

Criteria for Full Implementation Response

  • The organization has developed and executed a network segmentation strategy commensurate with the sensitivity levels of the systems and data. The assessment team should determine, collectively, the optimal network segmentation strategy for the system or application under assessment. If the system or application under assessment is reasonably isolated, in accordance with the optimal strategy, utilizing a variety of types of segmentation, the response should be graded “Full Implementation.”

Criteria for Partial Implementation Response

  • If the system or application under assessment is reasonably isolated, but there are additional types of segmentation that should be employed, the response should be graded “Partial Implementation.”
  • (Otherwise, the answer is marked as No Implementation)

Possible evidence

  • Network diagram depicting network segmentation, control implementation descriptions in the System Security Plan (SSP) describing the network segmentation types used to achieve the network segmentation

Reference to standards/source assessments

  • NIST 800-160, Rev. 1.
  • NIST 800-172: 3.13.4.e
  • NIST 800-53, Rev. 5: SC-3(2)

options.text: Isolate security functions from non-security functions
Isolate mission-focused components from business elements
Isolate elements based on function (e.g., application, storage, database)
Isolate production, development, testing, and staging environments, if applicable
Organization does not segment its network

questions.title: WI:SG-2.Q1
questions.text: Does the organization automatically isolate untrusted devices from production networks?
questions.supplemental:
Importance: An organization should constantly monitor and validate the security posture of devices connecting to the network.

Question Intent: Does the organization have the capability to automatically isolate untrusted devices from the production network(s), a key component of an optimized Zero Trust Architecture (ZTA) implementation.

Criteria for Full Implementation Response

  • The organization has the capability to automatically isolate all untrusted devices from the production network and has documented the capability in a policy, procedure, or in relevant control implementation descriptions in a System Security Plan (SSP).

Criteria for Partial Implementation Response

  • The organization enforces compliance for most devices, isolating untrusted devices from the production network and has documented the capability in a policy, procedure, or in relevant control implementation descriptions in a System Security Plan (SSP).
  • (Otherwise, the answer is marked as No Implementation)

Possible evidence

  • Policies, procedures, or System Security Plans (SSPs) that document the capability.

Reference to standards/source assessments

  • CISA Zero Trust Maturity Model
  • NIST 800-53, Rev. 5: SC-7(20), SC-7(21), SA-8(9)

questions.text:
(a) Determine criteria for unusual or unauthorized activities or conditions for inbound and outbound communications traffic;
(b) Monitor inbound and outbound communications traffic [Assignment: organization-defined frequency] for [Assignment: organization
questions.supplemental:
Importance: In order to respond to events in cyber-relevant time, an organization must have unified monitoring strategy that, when executed, provides a centralized entity with the ability maintain holistic awareness of the organization’s network and systems.

Question Intent: Determine if the organization has defined criteria for anomalous or unauthorized activities that should result in the generation of alerts. Does the organization monitor inbound and outbound traffic to identify anomalous or unauthorized activities?

Criteria for Partial Implementation Response

  •  (Otherwise, the answer is marked as No Implementation)

questions.title: WI:UN-1.Q1
questions.text: Does the organization require reauthentication at random intervals for? (Select all that apply)
questions.supplemental:
Importance: Reauthentication at random intervals or unpredictably maintains an environment of uncertainty for an adversary which results in an attacker taking more time or failing to successfully compromise targeted assets.

Question Intent: To determine if the organization has implemented the ability to reauthenticate at random intervals, all privileged and standard user accounts, and service accounts.

  • Change behavior or state at times that are determined randomly or by complex functions. Make changes randomly or unpredictably.
  • Randomness introduces increased levels of uncertainty for adversaries regarding the actions that organizations take to defend their systems against attacks.
  • Maintain an environment of uncertainty for the adversary and keep the adversary from extrapolating from past events. Such actions may impede the ability of adversaries to correctly target an organization’s mission critical information resources.

Criteria for Full Implementation Response

  • Reauthentication at random intervals of all critical service/HVA privileged and standard user accounts, and all service accounts has been implemented by the organization.

Criteria for Partial Implementation Response

  • Reauthentication at random intervals of some critical service/HVA privileged and standard user accounts, and some service accounts has been implemented by the organization.

Possible evidence

  • Documentation detailing the implementation and configuration of reauthentication techniques implemented using random intervals and applied to standard user accounts, privileged user accounts and service accounts.
  • Log files showing the reauthentication of user, privileged and service accounts occurring at random intervals.

Reference to standards/source assessments

  • NIST 800-53, Rev. 5: SC-30(2), CA-6
  • NIST 800-160, Rev. 1: Temporal Unpredictability

questions.title: RE:AN-1.Q1
questions.text: Are events managed and tracked to resolution?
questions.supplemental:
Importance: The organization should have a formal process for logging events as they are identified and for tracking and managing them through the incident lifecycle.

Question Intent: Determine if the organization manages and tracks events to resolution.

An event is one or more occurrences that affect assets and has the potential to disrupt the critical service.

Periodically (as defined by the organization) review the incident knowledge base for events that have not been closed or that do not have a disposition.

Events that have not been closed or that do not have a disposition should be reprioritized, analyzed, and tracked to resolution.

Criteria for Full Implementation Response

  • The organization should have a tracking knowledgebase/system to track events and incidents through their lifecycle.
  • Event and incident reports are documented.
  • The organization should establish and distribute standard reports with status information about events and incidents as they move through the lifecycle.
  • The organization manages and tracks all events to resolution.

Criteria for Partial Implementation Response

  • Events are documented and managed but not all are tracked to resolution.

Possible evidence

  • A report, list, or document that illustrates events being managed and tracked to resolution.

Reference to standards/source assessments

  • IMR: EH:G3.Q6.
  • CRR: IM:G2.Q7  
  • NIST 800-53, Rev. 5: AU-6, CA-7, IR-4, IR-5, PE-6, SI-4

questions.title: RE:AN-2.Q1
questions.text: Are incidents analyzed to determine a response?
questions.supplemental:
Importance: Incidents are analyzed to help the organization determine an appropriate response by examining the underlying causes and actions and the potential impact.

Question Intent: Determine if incidents are analyzed to determine a response.

  • Incident analysis should focus on properly defining the underlying problem, condition, or issue.
  • Incident analysis should help the organization prepare the most appropriate and timely response to the incident.
  • Incident analysis should determine whether the incident has second-order ramifications (e.g., operational, legal, regulatory, reputation).

Examples of incident analysis activities:

  • interviews with those who reported the underlying event(s) and were affected by it
  • interviews with specific knowledge experts
  • review of relevant logs and audit trails of network and physical activity
  • consultation of vulnerability and incident databases (US-CERT Vulnerability Notes Database / MITRE’s Common Vulnerabilities and Exposures List)
  • consultation with law enforcement, legal, audit, product vendors, and emergency management
  • timeline development
  • malware analysis
  • system forensics captures / imaging

Criteria for Full Implementation Response

  • A standardized and consistent incident analysis approach and structure is established
  • The organization analyzes all incidents to determine a response.

Criteria for Partial Implementation Response

  • Events and incidents are analyzed, but without standardized and consistent approach, or without documentation; OR
  • A standardized and consistent incident analysis approach and structure is documented, but it is not consistently used; OR
  • The organization analyzes some incidents but not all to determine a response

Possible evidence

  • Updated incident knowledgebase; incident analysis reports; reports from analysis tools and techniques.

Reference to standards/source assessments

  • IMR: IR:G2.Q1
  • CERT RMM IMC:SG3.SP2
  • NIST 800-53, Rev. 5: CP-2, IR-4

questions.title: RE:AN-5.Q1
questions.text: Have sources of vulnerability information been identified?
questions.supplemental:
Importance: Information about vulnerabilities is available from a wide variety of organizational and external sources. Identification and analysis of vulnerabilities are essential elements of managing vulnerabilities before they are exploited.

Question Intent: To determine if sources of vulnerability information have been identified.

  • Internal sources typically provide information about vulnerabilities that are unique to the organization.
  • Internal processes, such as incident management, could be an internal source of vulnerability information.
  • External or public sources typically provide information that is focused on common technologies.

Example sources of vulnerability information:

  • Vendors of software, systems, and hardware technologies
  • Common free catalogs, such as US-CERT Vulnerability Database and the Common Vulnerabilities and Exposures (CVE) List
  • Industry groups
  • Results of executing automated tools, techniques, and methods

Criteria for Full Implementation Response

  • The organization has identified and documented sources of vulnerability information for all of the assets that support the critical service.

Criteria for Partial Implementation Response

  • The organization has identified and documented sources of vulnerability information for some assets.

Possible evidence

  • List of sources of vulnerability information

Reference to standards/source assessments

  • CRR: VM:G2.Q1
  • NIST 800-53, Rev. 5: SI-5, PM-15

questions.title: RE:AM-1.Q1
questions.text: Does the organization maintain a documented continuous monitoring strategy/plan?
questions.supplemental:
Importance: Continuous monitoring at the organization level facilitates ongoing awareness of the security and privacy posture across the organization to support organizational risk management decisions. The terms continuous and ongoing imply that organizations assess and monitor their controls and risks at a frequency sufficient to support risk-based decisions. Different types of controls may require different monitoring frequencies. The results of continuous monitoring guide and inform risk response actions by organizations.

Question Intent: To determine if the organization has developed a continuous monitoring plan.

Such plans often include:

  1. Establishing organization-defined metrics to be monitored;
  1. Establishing frequencies for monitoring and assessment of control effectiveness;
  2. Ongoing monitoring of organization-defined metrics in accordance with the continuous monitoring strategy;
  3. Correlation and analysis of information generated by control assessments and monitoring;
  4. Response actions to address results of the analysis of control assessment and monitoring information; and
  1. Reporting the security and privacy status of organizational systems to organization-defined personnel or roles within the organization-defined frequency            

Discussion: Continuous monitoring programs allow organizations to maintain the authorizations of systems and common controls in highly dynamic environments of operation with changing mission and business needs, threats, vulnerabilities, and technologies. Having access to security- and privacy-related information on a continuing basis through reports and dashboards gives organizational officials the capability to make effective, timely, and informed risk management decisions, including ongoing authorization decisions. To further facilitate security and privacy risk management, organizations consider aligning organization-defined monitoring metrics with organizational risk tolerance as defined in the risk management strategy. Monitoring requirements, including the need for monitoring, may be referenced in other controls and control enhancements such as, AC-2g, AC-2(7), AC-2(12)(a), AC-2(7)(b), AC-2(7)(c), AC-17(1), AT-4a, AU-13, AU-13(1), AU-13(2), CA-7, CM-3f, CM-6d, CM-11c, IR-5, MA-2b, MA-3a, MA-4a, PE-3d, PE-6, PE-14b, PE-16, PE-20, PM-6, PM-23, PS-7e, SA-9c, SC-5(3)(b), SC-7a, SC-7(24)(b), SC-18b, SC-43b, SI-4.

Criteria for Full Implementation Response

  • The organization has a documented continuous monitoring plan.

Criteria for Partial Implementation Response

  • The organization has an informal or incompletely documented continuous monitoring plan.

Possible evidence

  • Continuous Monitoring strategy, program charter, or procedures

Reference to standards/source assessments

  • NIST 800-53, Rev. 5: PM-31

questions.title: RE:AM-2.Q1
questions.text: Are tools and/or methods employed for coordinating audit information among external organizations when information is transmitted across organizational boundaries?
questions.supplemental:
Importance: When organizations use systems or services of external organizations, the audit logging capability necessitates a coordinated, cross-organization approach. For example, maintaining the identity of individuals who request specific services across organizational boundaries may often be difficult, and doing so may prove to have significant performance and privacy ramifications. Therefore, it is often the case that cross-organizational audit logging simply captures the identity of individuals who issue requests at the initial system, and subsequent systems record that the requests originated from authorized individuals.

Question Intent: to determine if the organization has tools and/or methods that  they employ to coordinate audit information with external organizations when information is transmitted across organizational boundaries.

NIST 800-53 (AU-16): Employ organization-defined methods for coordinating audit information among external organizations when audit information is transmitted across organizational boundaries.

Criteria for Full Implementation Response

  • The organization has defined and documented methods for coordinating audit information with external organizations when audit  information is transmitted across organizational boundaries

Criteria for Partial Implementation Response

  • The organization coordinates audit information with  external organizations when audit  information is transmitted across organizational boundaries. However, the methods by which this process is performed are not defined and documented.

Possible evidence

  • Information Security Continuous Monitoring (ISCM) policy or procedure, auditing policy or procedure, information flow policy or diagram

Reference to standards/source assessments

  • NIST 800-53, Rev. 5: AU-16

questions.text: Are there staff (e.g. forensic and malware analysts, developers, and operations personnel, etc.) dedicated to analyzing indicators of compromise and adversary TTPs, including observed behavior, malware, and other artifacts left behind by adverse events.?

Importance: understanding the current threat landscape in industry and within an organization is crucial to informing defense efforts and tailoring existing security counter measures to better respond to incidents.

Question Intent: this question is seeking to understand what kind of staff exist for performing threat intelligence, digital forensics, incident response, threat hunting, and malware analysis functions within an organization.

Criteria for Full Implementation Response

  • The organization has staff with dedicated roles responsible for analyzing indicators of compromise, adversary TTPs, observed behavior, malware, and other artifacts left behind by adverse events within the organization.

Criteria for Partial Implementation Response

  • The organization has staff responsible for analyzing indicators of compromise, adversary TTPs, observed behavior, malware, and other artifacts left behind by adverse events within the organization. However, this is not their primary responsibility.

Possible evidence

  • Roles as described in the incident management plan, job descriptions of employees performing such work.

questions.title: RE:CO-3.Q1
questions.text: Are alerts and warnings applicable to ongoing incidents communicated to the internal and external stakeholders as necessary?
questions.supplemental:
Importance: Part of an effective incident management process is the ability to quickly disseminate the correct information to the right people at the right time. The internal and external stakeholders need to understand what threats or vulnerabilities might impact them, the associated level of risk, and how to protect against or mitigate them. Incident management personnel provide such notifications and warnings to promote awareness of threats and malicious activity and to help support organizational response actions.

Question Intent: To ensure that the incident management organization provide alerts, notifications, and warnings to promote awareness of relevant/active incidents for internal and external stakeholders.

  • For circumstances where stakeholder or user awareness or actions are necessary to help contain or remediate the incident, or prevent more widespread impact, it is essential to communicate these details effectively during the incident response process.
  • Incident management personnel work to provide such notifications and warnings to promote awareness of threats and malicious activity, and to help support organizational response actions. Depending on the mission of the incident management function, alerts and warnings may be shared with other relevant stakeholders and external parties.
  • Notifications, reports, and warnings should be distributed in a manner commensurate with the sensitivity of the information related to the activity. Sensitive information should be handled only through appropriate mechanisms.

Criteria for Full Implementation Response

  • The organization communicates alerts, notifications, and warnings for all ongoing incidents.

Criteria for Partial Implementation Response

  • The organization communicates alerts, notifications, and warnings for some incidents.

Possible evidence

  • Alerts, notifications, and warnings for ongoing incidents that include the stakeholder distribution list

Reference to standards/source assessments

  • IMR: IR:G3.Q6
  • NIST 800-53, Rev. 5: CA-2, CA-7, CP-2, IR-4, IR-8, PE-6, RA-5, SI-4

questions.title: RE:CO-4.Q1
questions.text: Is there a process to prioritize and transfer incidents to the appropriate queue, group, or personnel after formal incident declaration?
questions.supplemental:
Importance: Develop an incident escalation process. The incident escalation process should consider the type and extent of incident and the appropriate stakeholders. Incidents that the organization has declared and that require an organizational response must be escalated to those stakeholders who can implement, manage, and bring to closure an appropriate and timely solution. The organization must establish processes to ensure that incidents are referred to the appropriate stakeholders.

Question Intent: To determine if there is a process that prioritizes incidents, and guides the transfer to the appropriate group, or personnel for input and/or resolution.

  • Prioritization may be tied to the organization’s
  • risk appetite
  • impact to the organization
  • other organizationally defined prioritization criteria
  • Incidents that the organization has declared should be assigned to the appropriate queue, group, or personnel who can manage and resolve the incident.
  • The queue, group, or personnel can be internal to the organization (such as a standing incident response team or an incident-specific team) or external, in the form of contractors or other suppliers.

Criteria for Full Implementation Response

  • The organization has a process to prioritize all incidents and provides guidance on how to transfer incidents to the proper queue, group, or personnel for input and resolution.

Criteria for Partial Implementation Response

  • The organization has a process but does not include one of the following: a process to prioritize all incidents, or guidance on how to transfer them to the proper queue, group, or personnel for input and resolution.
  • Or, A process is in development and partially documented

Possible evidence

  • A documented process for prioritizing incidents and transferring incidents to the proper queue, group or personnel for input and resolution, results of process audits indicating that the process is being followed

questions.title: RE:CO-5.Q1
questions.text: Have external stakeholders (such as emergency management personnel, regulatory, and information sharing organizations) been identified to whom threat information must be communicated?
questions.supplemental:
RE:CO-5.Q1

Have external stakeholders (such as emergency management personnel, regulatory, and information sharing organizations) been identified to whom threat information must be communicated?

Importance: External stakeholders may have a stated role in communication plans, or the service continuity plans of the organization.

Question Intent: To determine if external stakeholders who must receive threat information have been identified.

  • External stakeholders are identified to:
  • ensure communications about ongoing threat monitoring activities
  • promote threat awareness
  • ensure that the organization and its external stakeholders are performing under a common operating picture
  • Examples of external stakeholders include:
  • first responders including law enforcement, fire, and medical
  • media including newspaper, television, radio, and internet
  • customers, business partners, and upstream suppliers
  • local, state, and federal emergency management
  • local utilities such as power, gas, telecommunications, and water
  • legal, regulatory, and governing agencies
  • Typical work products include:
  • list of external stakeholders and alternates
  • stakeholder contact information

Criteria for Full Implementation Response

  • All external stakeholders who must receive threat information have been identified and documented.

Criteria for Partial Implementation Response

  • Some external stakeholders have been identified and documented.

Possible evidence

  • List of external stakeholders and alternates, stakeholder contact information

Reference to standards/source assessments

  • CRR: SA:G2.Q2
  • NIST 800-53, Rev. 5: SI-5, PM-15

questions.title: RE:IM-1.Q1
questions.text: Do criteria exist for identifying incidents that require a post-incident review?
questions.supplemental:
Importance: It is important to develop these criteria with the stakeholders to ensure that post-incident reviews occur on all appropriate incidents, and do not consume unnecessary resources on those that do not meet the established thresholds.

Question Intent: To determine if there are documented criteria that guides the organization with determining which incidents require a post incident review.

  • This practice ensures that post-incident analysis meetings or reviews are held after significant incidents. The organization will use the criteria to help define “significant.”
  • The intent of these reviews is to identify any issues encountered or lessons learned, to propose areas for improvement, and to act on any findings or recommendations.

Examples of documented criteria:

  • departure from standard procedures
  • incidents of significant impact
  • incidents with unknown root cause
  • incidents of potential criminal activity
  • incidents of potential insider threat
  • incidents required by regulation to be reviewed

Criteria for Full Implementation Response

  • The organization uses documented criteria to evaluate all incidents for post incident review.

Criteria for Partial Implementation Response

  • The criteria for post-incident review is in development and partially documented.
  • Or, the criteria exist, but are used for only some incidents.

Possible evidence

  • A documented list of criteria for identifying incidents that require post-incident review.

Reference to standards/source assessments

  • IMR: PI:G1.Q1
  • NIST 800-53, Rev. 5: CP-2, IR-4, IR-8

questions.title: RE:IM-2.Q1
questions.text: Are lessons learned from post-incident review and analysis used to improve organizational asset protection and sustainment strategies?
questions.supplemental:
Importance: Lessons learned from post-incident review will help determine the validity and effectiveness of the organization’s current protection and sustainment strategies and are used to improve those strategies.

Question Intent: To determine if lessons learned are used to improve the organization’s asset protection and sustainment strategies.

  • Lessons learned from post-incident review should help determine the validity and effectiveness of the organization’s current strategies for protecting and sustaining assets.
  • Lessons learned can be extremely helpful in improving an organizations protection and sustainment strategies and the incident handling process itself.
  • A lessons-learned meeting or review should be held after a major incident with all stakeholders.
  • Lessons-learned data can be incorporated into the organization’s risk management process, ultimately leading to the selection and implementation of additional controls and improvements to the organization’s protection and sustainment strategies.

Criteria for Full Implementation Response

  • The organization uses lessons learned from all incidents that required post-incident review to improve asset protection and sustainment strategies.

Criteria for Partial Implementation Response

  • The organization uses lessons learned from some incidents that required post-incident review, to improve asset protection and sustainment strategies.
  • Or, the organization uses some lessons learned to improve asset protection and sustainment strategies.

Possible evidence

  • A report or document illustrating lessons learned from the knowledgebase or other source being used to improve organizational asset protection and sustainment strategies
  • Post-incident review minutes illustrating lessons learned being used to make changes to organizational artifacts for the purposes of improving asset protection and sustainment
  • Asset protection and sustainment strategy documentation with changes incorporated as a result of lessons learned

Reference to standards/source assessments

  • IMR: PI:G1.Q3
  • NIST 800-53, Rev. 5: CP-2, IR-4, IR-8

questions.title: RE:MI-1.Q1
questions.text: Are responses to declared incidents developed and implemented according to pre-defined procedures?
questions.supplemental:
Importance: Many events and incidents in organizations happen with great velocity and confusion depending on the complexity and nature.   Organizations must define what constitutes and event and identify the indications of events turning into incidents.   To facilitate rapid reaction and response to maintain operational resilience, the organization should document these criteria in a formal a detailed manner.

Question Intent: To determine if responses to declared incidents are developed and implemented according to pre-defined procedures.

  • The organization’s response to an incident should be founded on pre-defined incident response procedures.
  • Pre-defined procedures describe the actions the organization takes to prevent or contain the impact of an incident.
  • Incident response may be as simple as notifying users to avoid opening a specific type of email message or as complicated as having to implement service continuity plans.

The actions related to incident response can include:

  • containing damage (i.e., taking hardware or systems offline or by locking-down a facility)
  • collecting evidence (including logs and audit trails)
  • interviewing relevant staff
  • communicating to stakeholders
  • developing and implementing corrective actions and controls
  • implementing continuity and restoration plans or other emergency actions

Criteria for Full Implementation Response

  • The organization uses predefined procedures to develop and implement a response to all declared incidents.

Criteria for Partial Implementation Response

  • The organization may have predefined procedures.   However, the procedures may not be written in a clear nature. Vague direction could lead to poor interpretation and delayed response as a result.

Possible evidence

  • Organizational policy and procedures related to incident management
  • Documentation and/or logs that demonstrate proper and reliable response to identified incidents
  • Criteria for incidents are clearly defined and easy to act upon

Reference to standards/source assessments

  • CRR: IM:G4.Q2. 
  • NIST 800-53, Rev. 5: IR-4

questions.title: RE:MI-1.Q2
questions.text: Are incidents managed and tracked to resolution?
questions.supplemental:
Importance: Tracking incidents to closure provides a mechanism for the organization to know what incidents are still open and are in need further effort to resolve.  This also provides an indication to all relevant stakeholders that no further actions are required or outstanding for the incident.

Question Intent: To determine if incidents are tracked and managed to resolution.

  • Incidents may be open for an extended period of time, may not have followed the organization’s incident management process or may not have been formally closed.
  • The organization should have a process for the formal closure of incidents that results in formally logging a status of “closed” in the incident knowledge base.
  • The status of incidents in the incident knowledge base should be reviewed regularly to determine if open incidents should be closed or need additional action.

Typical work products include:

  • criteria for incident closure
  • incident closure reports
  • updated incident knowledgebase

Criteria for Full Implementation Response

  • The organization tracks and manages all incidents to resolution.

Criteria for Partial Implementation Response

  • The organization tracks and manages some incidents to resolution.

Possible evidence

  • Incident status reports or knowledgebase detailing the status of all incidents.  This report should clearly designate whether the incident has been closed or is still in some form of open status.

Reference to standards/source assessments

  • IMR: IR:G3.Q7
  • NIST 800-53, Rev. 5: IR-4, IR-5, AU-6

questions.title: RE:MI-2.Q1
questions.text: Are actions taken to manage exposure to identified vulnerabilities?
questions.supplemental:
Importance: Managing and remediating legitimate vulnerabilities will help protect the organization from potential attach by adversaries.

Question Intent: To determine if actions are taken to manage exposure to identified vulnerabilities.

The organization must develop and implement a resolution strategy to manage exposure from identified vulnerabilities.

The resolution strategy may include actions to:

  • Minimize the organization’s exposure to the vulnerability (by reducing the likelihood that the vulnerability will be exploited).

Actions taken to manage exposure may include:

  • implementing software, systems, and firmware patches
  • developing and implementing operational workarounds
  • developing and implementing new protective controls
  • updating existing controls
  • developing and implementing new service continuity plans, or updating existing plans

Criteria for Full Implementation Response

  • The organization takes action to manage exposure to all identified vulnerabilities for all of the assets that support the critical service/HVA environment.

Criteria for Partial Implementation Response

  • The organization takes action to manage exposure to some identified vulnerabilities.
  • Or; the organization takes action to manage exposure to all identified vulnerabilities for some assets that support the critical service/HVA environment.

Possible evidence

  • Vulnerability management strategies or action plans
  • Updated vulnerability repository, with resolution status information
  • Vulnerability management process status reports

Reference to standards/source assessments

  • CRR: VM:G3.Q2.
  • NIST 800-53, Rev. 5: CA-7, RA-3, RA-5

questions.title: RE:RD-1.Q1
questions.text: How are backup and storage procedures for high-value information assets tested? (Select one)
questions.supplemental:
Importance: Periodic testing of the organization’s backup and storage procedures ensures continued validity as operational conditions change.

Question Intent: To determine how or if backup and storage procedures for high-value information assets are tested.

  • Organizations need assurance that backup information can be reliably retrieved. Reliability pertains to the systems and system components where the backup information is stored, the operations used to retrieve the information, and the integrity of the information being retrieved.
  • Independent and specialized tests can be used for each of the aspects of reliability. For example, decrypting and transporting (or transmitting) a random sample of backup files from the alternate storage or backup site and comparing the information to the same information at the primary processing site can provide such assurance.
  • Testing of backup and storage procedures is done to ensure the requirements of the critical service/HVA are being met.
  • Information asset backup and storage procedures typically include:
  • frequency standards
  • retention periods
  • authorized storage locations and methods
  • encryption and protection requirements
  • testing standards
  • periodic review and revision of backup and storage procedures
  • System-level information includes system state information, operating system software, middleware, application software, and licenses.
  • User-level information includes information other than system-level information.
  • System backups reflect the requirements in contingency plans as well as other organizational requirements for backing up information.

Criteria for Full Implementation Response

  • The organization conducts formal disaster recovery exercises that include cutting the production version of the service over to an alternate version of the service (Item 1).

Criteria for Partial Implementation Response

  • The organization conducts formal disaster recovery exercises that restore high-value assets into a test environment for testing (Item 2).
  • Or, limited full restoration that is reviewed for accuracy and functionality (Item 3).
  • Or, ad hoc restoration of backups as part of normal operations (Item 4).

Possible evidence

  • Documented backup and storage procedures
  • Documented test results

Reference to standards/source assessments

  • NIST 800-53, Rev. 5: CP-9(1)

options.text: Formal disaster recovery exercises that cut production network over to restored capability
Formal disaster recovery exercises that restore high-value assets into a test environment for testing
Limited full restoration that is reviewed for accuracy and functionality.
Ad hoc restoration of backups as part of normal operations

questions.title: RE:RD-2.Q1
questions.text: Does the organization manage capacity, bandwidth, or other redundancy to limit the effects of information flooding denial-of-service attacks?
questions.supplemental:
Importance: Capacity management can be done to ensure that sufficient capacity bandwidth and/or other redundancy is available to counter flooding attacks.

Question Intent: To determine if capacity management is done with the intention or requirement of limiting the effects of information flooding attacks.

  • Denial-of-service events may occur due to a variety of internal and external causes, such as an attack by an adversary or a lack of planning to support organizational needs with respect to capacity and bandwidth
  • Employing increased network capacity and bandwidth combined with service redundancy can reduce the susceptibility to denial-of-service events.
  • Managing capacity ensures that sufficient capacity is available to counter flooding attacks.
  • Managing capacity includes establishing selected usage priorities, quotas, partitioning, or load balancing

Criteria for Full Implementation Response

  • The organization performs capacity management and planning for all assets that support the critical service/HVA in such a manner to limit the effects of information flooding (denial of service) attacks.

Criteria for Partial Implementation Response

  • The organization performs capacity management and planning for some assets that support the critical service/HVA, 
  • OR
  • The capacity management strategy to limit the effects of information flooding (denial of service) attacks is in development and partially documented.

Possible evidence

  • Documented capacity management strategy detailing the approach to limit the effects of information flooding (denial of service) attacks.
  • Capacity forecasts, statistics and performance metrics used to inform the strategy to limit the effects of information flooding attacks.

Reference to standards/source assessments

  • NIST 800-53, Rev. 5: SC-5(2)

references.title: NIST SP 800-53 Rev. 5: Security and Privacy Controls for Information Systems and Organizations

questions.title: RE:RD-3.Q1
questions.text: Can the organization perform its essential functions if its primary processing and storage capabilities are unavailable?
questions.supplemental:
Importance: Having alternate processing and storage capabilities allows an organization to sustain the critical service/HVA despite compromise, failure, or disruption.

Question Intent: To determine if the organization can sustain the critical service/HVA  operations if the primary processing and storage capability   is unavailable.

  • Plan for the transfer of mission critical business functions to alternate processing and/or storage sites with minimal or no loss of operational continuity. Sustain that continuity until the restoration of the mission critical business functions to primary processing and/or storage sites.
  • Organizations may choose to conduct contingency planning activities for alternate processing and storage sites as part of business continuity planning or business impact analyses. Primary processing and/or storage sites defined by organizations as part of contingency planning may change depending on the circumstances associated with the contingency
  • Alternate storage sites are geographically distinct from primary storage sites and maintain duplicate copies of information and data if the primary storage site is not available.
  • Similarly, alternate processing sites are geographically distinct from primary processing sites and provide processing capability if the primary processing site is not available.
  • Alternate processing and storage sites reflect the requirements in contingency plans so that organizations can maintain essential mission and business functions despite compromise, failure, or disruption in organizational systems

Criteria for Full Implementation Response

  • The critical service/HVA essential functions are fully sustained if its primary processing and storage capabilities are unavailable.

Criteria for Partial Implementation Response

  • The critical service/HVA essential functions are partially sustained if its primary processing and storage capabilities are unavailable.

Possible evidence

  • Documentation detailing the implementation and configuration of alternate processing and storage capabilities
  • Contracts or agreements for the maintenance of a hot site, warm site, or cold site.

Reference to standards/source assessments

  • NIST 800-53, Rev. 5: CP-2, CP-7

questions.title: AD:RP-1.Q2
questions.text: Are recovery activities performed in accordance with the recovery plans?
questions.supplemental:
Importance: Recovery plans that are not regularly exercised may not be able to be executed in a timely or complete manner consistent with the intent of the recovery plans.

Question Intent: The goal of this question is to determine if the plans provide sufficient process direction to be fully executed to achieve the recovery time and point objectives.

  • Exercised plans are executed in accordance with the plans themselves.

Criteria for Full Implementation Response

  • Plan exists
  • Plan is regularly evaluated and updated as needed
  • Plan is regularly exercised to ensure operational capability
  • Recovery exercises are completed in fully accordance with the tested plan
  • Tested plan achieves recovery time objective as stated in the plan
  • Tested plan achieves recovery point objective as stated in the plan

Criteria for Partial Implementation Response

  • Failure to meet recovery time or point objectives; 
     OR
  • Incomplete direction within the plan to facilitate execution

Possible Evidence

  • Recovery plan(s), evidence of recovery plan reviews and updates

Reference to standards/source assessments

  • NIST 800-53, Rev. 5: CP-4(4)

questions.title: AD:IM-1.Q2
questions.text: Are recovery and continuity improvements identified as a result of executing service continuity plans?
questions.supplemental:
Importance: As systems evolve so too must plans designed to provide continuity of service capabilities. Without current service continuity plans the organization may not be able to ensure recovery of mission essential services.

Question Intent: This question is presented to ascertain the current relevance of documented service continuity plans and to determine if improvements are identified as a result of executing service continuity plans.

  • As a result of the review of executed service continuity plans areas of improvement are identified, captured, and documented.
  • Typical work products include:
  • list of improvements to service continuity plans
  • list of improvements to service continuity test plans

Criteria for “Yes” Response

  • Improvements to each executed service continuity plan that supports the critical service are identified and documented.
     OR
  • If service continuity plans have not been executed, the identification of improvements to executed plans is required as part of a standard process.

Criteria for “Incomplete” Response

  • Improvements to some executed service continuity plans are identified and documented.

Possible Evidence

  • Change management documentation for service continuity plans

Reference to standards/source assessments

  • CRR: SCM:G4.Q3
  • NIST 800-53, Rev. 5: IR-4, CP-2

questions.title: AD:CO-3.Q2
questions.text: Are internal and external stakeholders to which the organization must communicate relative to incident response and service continuity activities  identified?
questions.supplemental:
Importance: Organizations have many types of stakeholders that require communications related to managing incidents and recovery activities. These stakeholders may be very diverse depending on the type of communications needs they have, the frequency of the communications (whether discrete or continuous, circumstantial, or ongoing), and the level of communications necessary (notifications, press releases, crisis communications, etc.). Understanding the level and extent of stakeholders helps the organization to effectively develop and satisfy communications requirements.

Question Intent: To determine whether the organization has identified the internal and external stakeholders with whom communication must occur during incident management and recovery activities.

Internal stakeholders are identified to ensure ongoing communication about the organization’s activities, promote awareness, and ensure that staff can effectively communicate and collaborate during disruptive events. Likewise, external stakeholders may need information about the organization’s incident response, or they may have to be able to effectively communicate with the organization during times of crisis. These external organizations may even have a stated role in the communications plans or the service continuity of the organization. In addition, some regulatory and legal entities may require ongoing communications as evidence that an organization has taken appropriate actions to prepare for specific threats such as natural disasters and terrorism. Thus, the list of external stakeholders is developed to ensure proactive communications and message delivery regarding the organization’s preparedness and capabilities for managing incidents and recovery.

Because there are many stakeholders that require information, the organization must identify the relevant stakeholders and distribute information about communications plans to them as necessary. These stakeholders will have a vested interest or vital role in communications about incident management and recovery activities.

When determining which stakeholders to include in the list, consider

  • rationale for stakeholder involvement
  • roles and responsibilities of the relevant stakeholders
  • relationships between stakeholders
  • relative importance of the stakeholder to the success of the program
  • resources (e.g., training, materials, time, and funding) needed to ensure stakeholder interaction

Criteria for Full Implementation Response

  • All primary stakeholders requiring communications are identified and formally documented.

Criteria for Partial Implementation Response

  • Some primary stakeholders requiring communications are identified and formally documented. (Otherwise, the answer is marked as No Implementation)

Possible Evidence

  • List of stakeholders that need to receive communications
  • Classes or roles of stakeholders
  • List of appropriate internal and external stakeholders
  • Stakeholder involvement plan

Reference to standards/source assessments

  • CERT RMM COMM:SG1.SP1
  • NIST 800-53, Rev. 5: CP-2, IR-4

questions.title: AD:RL-1.Q2
questions.text: Is there a process of designating a resource external to the organization or system as trusted?
questions.supplemental:
Importance: Ensuring there is a mission or business reason for trusting a resource prevents the associated trustworthiness from being inadvertently diminished and may prevent the trust from being consequently misplaced.

Question Intent: To determine if the process for designating a resource (such as a workstation, network, application, or database, etc.) as trusted ensures that a mission or business reason exists to justify the designation.

Trustworthiness: Worthy of being trusted to fulfill whatever critical requirements may be needed for a particular component, subsystem, system, network, application, mission, business function, enterprise, or other entity.

  • Ensure that cyber resources are used consistently with mission or business function purposes and approved uses. Avoid “mission creep,” which can increase a system’s attack surface.
  • The principle of trusted components states that a component is trustworthy to at least a level commensurate with the security dependencies it supports (i.e., how much it is trusted to perform its security functions by other components).
  • Trustworthiness requirements can include attributes of safety, security, reliability, dependability, performance, resilience, and survivability under a wide range of potential adversity in the form of disruptions, hazards, and threats.

Criteria for Full Implementation Response

  • A process for designating a critical service/HVA resource as trusted has been implemented and documented.
  • And, the process ensures that there is a mission or business reason that justifies the designation of trusted.

Criteria for Partial Implementation Response

  • A process for designating a critical service/HVA resource as trusted is in development and partially documented.
     OR
  • The process is implemented but does not always ensure that there is a mission or business reason that justifies the designation of trusted.

 

Possible Evidence

  • A documented process for designating a critical service/HVA resource as trusted and ensuring that there is a mission or business reason that justifies the designation of trusted.
  • Documented outcomes of the process detailing the evaluation and mission/business reason for the designation of trusted.

Reference to standards/source assessments

  • NIST 800-53, Rev. 5: SA-8(9)

questions.title: AD:RL-2.Q2
questions.text: Does the organization have a formal policies or directives that govern outsourcing of essential and nonessential functions?
questions.supplemental:
nonessential functions?

Importance: A policy establishes and communicates the organizational expectations for planning and governing the outsourcing of essential and nonessential functions to the organization.

Question Intent: To determine if a policy that governs outsourcing of essential and nonessential functions exists.

  • A policy is a written communication from the organization’s senior management to employees.
  • It establishes the organizational expectations for planning and governing the outsourcing of essential and nonessential functions and communicates those expectations to the organization.

The policy should address:

  • responsibility, authority, ownership, and the requirement to perform outsourcing activities
  • establishment of procedures, standards, and guidelines
  • establishing and maintaining the outsourcing relationship
  • governing the outsourcing of essential and nonessential functions
  • measuring adherence to policy, exceptions granted, and policy violations
  • compliance with legal, regulatory, contractual, and government obligations
  • Offloading supportive but nonessential functions to other systems or to an external provider that is better able to perform the functions securely
  • Offloading to reduce the attack surface and motivate ongoing consideration of what is essential.

Criteria for Full Implementation Response

  • The organization has a documented policy for governing the outsourcing of essential and nonessential functions.

Criteria for Partial Implementation Response

  • A policy is in development and partially documented.

Possible Evidence

  • A documented policy for governing the outsourcing of essential and nonessential functions.

Reference to standards/source assessments:

  • NIST 800-53, Rev. 5: SA-9(1)

questions.title: AD:RL-3.Q2
questions.text: Does the organization require attack surface reviews of newly developed systems, system components, and system services?
questions.supplemental:
Importance: Attack surfaces review enable personnel to understand and address the systems and system components that present exposed areas that make those systems more vulnerable to attacks.

Question Intent: To determine if the organization require attack surface reviews of newly developed systems, system components, and system services.

  • Attack surfaces of systems and system components are exposed areas that make those systems more vulnerable to attacks.
  • Attack surfaces include any accessible areas where weaknesses or deficiencies in the hardware, software, and firmware components provide opportunities for adversaries to exploit vulnerabilities.
  • Attack surface reviews ensure that developers analyze the design and implementation changes to systems and mitigate attack vectors generated as a result of the changes.
  • The correction of identified flaws includes deprecation of unsafe functions.

Criteria for Full Implementation Response

  • The organization requires an attach surface review for all newly developed systems, system components and system services that support the critical service/HVA environment.

Criteria for Partial Implementation Response

  • The organization requires an attach surface review for some of the newly developed systems, system components and system services.

Possible Evidence

  • For all newly developed systems, system components and system services there should be a documented attack surface review and associated results.

Reference to standards/source assessments

  • NIST 800-53, Rev. 5: SA-11(6)

references.title: NIST SP 800-53 Rev. 5: Security and Privacy Controls for Information Systems and Organizations

questions.title: AN:AR-1.Q2
questions.text: Are staff with the necessary skill sets or automated systems available to make the changes?
questions.supplemental:
Importance: Staff that do not possess the necessary skills to perform configuration changes may cause extended outages or introduce errors into the system. Automated systems may mitigate this risk by providing consistency

Question Intent: Determine if there are staff members available to perform the required changes, or configure the available automated systems, to perform required changes.

Criteria for Full Implementation Response

  • The organization has a staffing plan in place that includes a list of required skills necessary to fulfill the needs of each position performing system reconfiguration, to include, if applicable, maintenance of any automated systems.

Criteria for Partial Implementation Response

  • Ad hoc configuration support without clearly defined skillsets.

Possible Evidence

  • Staffing plan and or automated system identified in a System Security Plan.

Reference to standards/source assessments

  • NIST 800-53, Rev. 5: AT-3

references.title: NIST SP 800-53 Rev. 5: Security and Privacy Controls for Information Systems and Organizations

questions.title: AN:AR-2.Q2
questions.text: Does the organization employ load balancing capability in front of critical applications or services?
questions.supplemental:
Importance: Service or application outages may be caused by over utilization. Load balancing across multiple systems reduces this risk.

Question Intent: Does the system have a load balancing solution to help reduce the risk of resource exhaustion?  If the organization outsources critical application or service support to a service provider, then the question applies to the service provider.

Criteria for Full Implementation Response

  • The organization employs load balancers for all critical application and service application.

Criteria for Partial Implementation Response

  • The organization has a load balancing configuration that does not consider the criticality of applications or resources.

Possible Evidence

  • Specific implementation details in a System Security Plan (SSP)

Reference to standards/source assessments

  • NIST 800-53, Rev. 5: SC-5(2)

references.title: NIST SP 800-53 Rev. 5: Security and Privacy Controls for Information Systems and Organizations

questions.title: AN:AR-3.Q2
questions.text: Does the organization employ a capability to adapt authentication based on factors such as location, device status, end user behavior, etc.?
questions.supplemental:
Importance: Anomalous login behavior such as out of hour logins, unreasonable times and distance between login attempts, or login duration may be indicators or attack or compromise.

Question Intent: Determine if the system is capable of assessing suspicious behavior and requiring additional authentication information. Organizations may employ specific techniques or mechanisms and establish protocols to assess suspicious behavior. Suspicious behavior may include accessing information that individuals do not typically access as part of their duties, roles, or responsibilities; accessing greater quantities of information than individuals would routinely access; or attempting to access information from suspicious network addresses. When pre-established conditions or triggers occur, organizations can require individuals to provide additional authentication information. Another potential use for adaptive authentication is to increase the strength of mechanism based on the number or types of records being accessed. 

Criteria for Full Implementation Response

  • The system monitors for, identifies suspicious behavior and under specified conditions requires additional authentication information.

Criteria for Partial Implementation Response

  • The system has the capability to identify anomalous login behavior but not to automatically require additional authentication information.

Possible Evidence

  • Specific implementation details in a System Security Plan (SSP).

Reference to standards/source assessments

questions.text: Does the organization require individuals accessing the system to employ organization-defined supplemental authentication techniques or mechanisms under specific organization-defined circumstances or situations?

Question Intent: to determine if the organization requires supplemental authentication techniques or mechanisms when accessing information systems under specific organization-defined circumstances or situations

questions.text:
Does the organization:
(a) Periodically review the privileges assigned to users to validate the need for such privileges?

Question Intent: This question seeks to ascertain whether the organizations service continuity plan is capable of sustaining continuity until full system restoration at primary processing and/or storage sites.

Criteria for Partial Implementation Response

Question Intent: This question determines whether the organization conducts penetration testing on organization-defined systems or system components in accordance with an organization defined frequency or schedule.

Criteria for Partial Implementation Response

questions.title: AN:DI-2.Q2
questions.text:
Does the organization Implement multi-factor authentication for local, network, or remote access to privileged accounts; non-privileged accounts such that:
(a) One of the factors is provided by a device separate from the system gaining access; and
(b) The device meets organization-defined strength of mechanism requirements.
questions.supplemental:
Importance: Regardless of the type of access (i.e., local, network, remote), privileged and non-privileged accounts are authenticated using multi-factor options appropriate for the level of risk. Implementing one of the factors on a separate device (e.g., a hardware token), provides a greater strength of mechanism and an increased level of assurance in the authentication process.

Question Intent: This question determines if one of the factors in the organizations multi-factor authentication process is provided by a device separate from the system to which the user is attempting to gain access (e.g., a hardware token).

The purpose of requiring a device that is separate from the system to which the user is attempting to gain access for one of the factors during multi-factor authentication is to reduce the likelihood of compromising authenticators or credentials stored on the system. 

Adversaries may be able to compromise such authenticators or credentials and subsequently impersonate authorized users. 

Criteria for Full Implementation Response

  • For both privileged and non-privileged accounts, the organization’s multi-factor authentication process for local, network and remote access ensures that one of the factors is provided by a device separate from the system to which the user is attempting to gain access
  • And, the device meets organization-defined strength of mechanism requirements

Criteria for Partial Implementation Response

  • The organization is in the process of implementing a multi-factor authentication process for local, network and remote access that ensures that one of the factors is provided by a device separate from the system to which the user is attempting to gain access.
  • Or, the multi-factor authentication process (that ensures that one of the factors is provided by a device separate from the system to which the user is attempting to gain access) exists and is only applied to either privileged or non-privileged accounts but not both.
  • Or, the multi-factor authentication process that ensures that one of the factors is provided by a device separate from the system to which the user is attempting to gain access) exists but does not meet organization-defined strength of mechanism requirements. 

Possible Evidence

  • Configuration documentation detailing the multi-factor authentication process and setup and showing that one of the factors is provided by a device separate from the system to which the user is attempting to gain access.
  • Configuration documentation detailing that the separate authentication device meets organization-defined strength of mechanism requirements.

Reference to standards/source assessments

  • NIST 800-53, Rev. 5: IA-2(6)

questions.title: AN:DI-3.Q2
questions.text: Does the organization require a diverse set of sources for organizational systems, system components, and services?
questions.supplemental:
Importance: Diversifying the supply of systems, system components, and services can reduce the impact of a supply chain event or compromise.

Question Intent: This question determines if the organization require a diverse set of sources for organizational systems, system components, and services. 

Diversifying the supply of systems, system components, and services can reduce the probability that adversaries will successfully identify and target the supply chain and can reduce the impact of a supply chain event or compromise.

Identifying multiple suppliers for replacement components can reduce the probability that the replacement component will become unavailable. 

Employing a diverse set of developers or logistics service providers can reduce the impact of a natural disaster or other supply chain event. 

Criteria for Full Implementation Response

  • The organization has established and documented a diverse set of sources for organizational systems, system components, and services.

Criteria for Partial Implementation Response

  • A diverse set of sources for organizational systems, system components, and services is in development and partially documented.
  • (Otherwise, the answer is marked as No Implementation)

Possible Evidence

  • A documented list of diverse sources for organizational systems, system components and services.

Reference to standards/source assessments

  • NIST 800-53, Rev. 5: SR-3(1)

questions.title: AN:DP-1.Q2
questions.text: Does the organization dynamically relocate sensors and monitoring capabilities to different network locations when organization-defined conditions or circumstances  that require it are met?
questions.supplemental:
Importance: Adversaries may take various paths and use different approaches as they move laterally through an organization (including its systems) to reach their target or as they attempt to exfiltrate information from the organization. The organization often only has a limited set of monitoring and detection capabilities, and they may be focused on the critical or likely infiltration or exfiltration paths. By using communications paths that the organization typically does not monitor, the adversary can increase its chances of achieving its desired goals. By relocating its sensors or monitoring capabilities to new locations, the organization can impede the adversary’s ability to achieve its goals. The relocation of the sensors or monitoring capabilities might be done based on threat information that the organization has acquired or randomly to confuse the adversary and make its lateral transition through the system or organization more challenging.

Question Intent: Does threat intelligence inform the planning and execution of information security continuous monitoring. Does the organization deploy sensors based to specific locations based on expected adversary activities?

Criteria for Full Implementation Response

  • The organization relocates sensors and monitoring capabilities to different network locations based on available threat intelligence and in accordance with strategy, policy, or procedures.

Criteria for Partial Implementation Response

  • The organization is developing strategy, policy, or procedures to relocate sensors and monitoring capabilities to different network locations based on conditions or circumstances.

Possible Evidence

  • Network diagrams and/or strategy, policy, or procedures describing the relocation of sensors or monitoring capabilities based on conditions or circumstances.

Reference to standards/source assessments

  • NIST 800-53, Rev. 5: SC-48, SC-48(1)

questions.title: AN:DP-2.Q2
questions.text: Does the organization distribute processing and storage components across multiple physical locations and logical domains?
questions.supplemental:
Importance: Distributing processing and storage across multiple physical locations or logical domains provides a degree of redundancy or overlap for organizations. The redundancy and overlap increase the work factor of adversaries to adversely impact organizational operations, assets, and individuals. The use of distributed processing and storage does not assume a single primary processing or storage location. Therefore, it allows for parallel processing and storage.

Question Intent: This question determines if the organization distributes processing and storage components across multiple physical locations and logical domains.

Criteria for Full Implementation Response

  • The organization distributes processing and storage across multiple physical locations or logical domains in accordance with a strategy, plan, concept of operation, or policy. As applicable, the specific implementation details are documented in a System Security Plan (SSP).

Criteria for Partial Implementation Response

  • The organization distributes processing and storage across multiple physical location or logical domains but has not documented its approach or the specific implementation details in a System Security Plan (SSP).
  • (Otherwise, the answer is marked as No Implementation)

Possible Evidence

  • An organizational strategy, plan, concept of operation, or policy. As applicable, specific implementation details in a System Security Plan (SSP).

Reference to standards/source assessments

  • NIST 800-53, Rev. 5: SC-36

questions.title: AN:GV-1.Q2
questions.text: Is there a documented policy for controls management?
questions.supplemental:
Importance: Organizations should have a documented policy for controls management as it establishes the organizational expectations for planning and performing the controls management process as well as communicates those expectations to the organization.

Question Intent: This question determines if a policy for performing controls management activities exists.

A policy is a written communication from the organization’s senior management to employees.

The controls management policy should address:

  • responsibility, authority, ownership, and the requirement to perform controls management activities
  • establishment of procedures, standards, and guidelines
  • requirements for periodically assessing the control environment
  • measuring adherence to policy, exceptions granted, and policy violations
  • compliance with legal, regulatory, contractual, and government obligations

Criteria for Full Implementation Response

  • The organization has a documented policy for performing controls management.

Criteria for Partial Implementation Response

  • A policy is in development and partially documented
  • (Otherwise, the answer is marked as No Implementation)

Possible Evidence

  • A Standard Operating Procedure for Controls Management or Other relevant organizational policy covering controls management.

Reference to standards/source assessments

  • CRR: CM:MIL2.Q2
  • NIST 800-53, Rev. 5: SC-1, SI-1, AC-1

questions.title: AN:GV-3.Q2
questions.text: Has the acquirer identified and documented baseline (boilerplate) requirements that apply to any supplier that supports the critical service?
questions.supplemental:
Importance: Consistency across multiple supplier contracts can help the acquirer achieve a higher degree of predictability and control among external entities and help to ensure that all suppliers meet at least a minimal level of requirements.

Question Intent: This question determines if the acquirer has established a set of baseline requirements that apply to all formal agreements with suppliers that support the critical service.

Developing baseline requirements normally involves an evaluation of the acquirer’s enterprise requirements. These are the requirements that the enterprise deems important for every supplier relationship. Regulatory requirements may often form the basis for these. For example, in the medical field, laws to protect the confidentiality of protected health information (PHI) require standard requirements for every third party that stores this information.

Typical work products:

  • Standard contract language that includes, for example, reporting, compliance, and flow down requirements

Criteria for Full Implementation Response

  • The acquirer has a documented collection of baseline contractual requirements for suppliers that support the critical service.

Criteria for Partial Implementation Response

  • The acquirer has a partially documented collection of baseline contractual requirements for suppliers, or the baseline requirements apply to only some suppliers, or the practice appears otherwise incomplete.
  • (Otherwise, the answer is marked as No Implementation)

Possible Evidence

  • Contracts between the supplier and acquirer.

Reference to standards/source assessments

  • NIST 800-53, Rev. 5: SR-3(3), SA-4

questions.title: AN:GV-4.Q2
questions.text: Is there adequate funding to perform controls management activities as planned?

Importance: Funding is an indication of higher-level management support and sponsorship of controls management activities.

Question Intent: This question determines if adequate funding has been provided for controls management activities. The intent of the question is to evaluate the completeness of the funding, not the completeness of the plan.

Funding should be available to support the proper oversight, execution, and maintenance of controls management activities.

Considerations for funding planned controls management activities include:

  • defining funding needs
  • establishing a budget
  • resolving funding gaps
  • funding the process activities including staffing, tools, training, etc.

Criteria for Full Implementation Response

  • Adequate funding has been provided to perform all planned controls management activities.

Criteria for Partial Implementation Response

  • The planned activities have only been partially funded.
  • (Otherwise, the answer is marked as No Implementation) 

Possible Evidence

  • Attestation from stakeholders regarding funding for controls management activities.

questions.text: Do documented procedures exist for either conducting the security risk assessment (RA) (e.g., COBIT, OCTAVE) or contracting with a third party to conduct it, and for analyzing the security risk assessment results?
questions.supplemental:

Question Intent: This question determines if procedures to either conduct or contract RAs are documented as well as documentation for analyzing the security RA results.

Criteria for Full Implementation Response

  • There exist documented procedures for either conducting the security RA or contracting with a third party to conduct it, and for analyzing the security RA results.

Criteria for Partial Implementation Response

  • There exist documented procedures for either conducting the security RA or contracting with a third party to conduct it, and for analyzing the security RA results.
  • (Otherwise, the answer is marked as No Implementation)

Possible Evidence

  • Copy of security RA program, policy, procedures, or guidance
  • Copies of security RA results and improvement/mitigation actions
  • List of security RA types and providers
  • Letter, email, or policy giving approval for security RAs to be conducted
  • Mechanisms for requesting assistance

questions.title: AN:RA-5.Q2
questions.text: Are risks are evaluated against risk tolerances and criteria?
questions.supplemental:
Importance: To determine the extent of the operational risk, the consequences of the risk must be evaluated using the organization’s risk measurement criteria. Not all risks are the same for all organizations; what might be a major concern for one organization might be minor for another for many reasons, such as financial solvency, market position, cash reserves, and industry.

Question Intent: This question determines if there is an evaluation of risk against the organizations risk tolerances and criteria.

Criteria for Full Implementation Response

  • Each risk is evaluated and assigned values in accordance with the defined risk parameters and risk measurement criteria, including risk tolerances.

Criteria for Partial Implementation Response

  • Not all risk is evaluated and assigned values in accordance with the defined risk parameters and risk measurement criteria, including risk tolerances..
  • (Otherwise, the answer is marked as No Implementation)

Possible Evidence

  • Updated risk statements with impact valuation

questions.title: AN:SC-1.Q2
questions.text: Has a plan for managing supply chain risk been established and agreed to by Stakeholders?
questions.supplemental:
Importance: Stakeholder buy-in for a supply chain risk management plan is critical to ensure that there is a champion for the plan, as well as general awareness within the organization.

Question Intent: This question determines if the acquirer has a plan for managing operational risk.

An operational risk management plan provides a common foundation for the performance of risk management activities. For External Dependencies Management, having a plan that includes external dependencies helps to coordinate management of these risks with the acquirer’s risk appetite and broader risk strategy.

Operational risk is defined as the potential impact on assets and their related services that could result from inadequate or failed internal processes, failures of systems or technology, deliberate or inadvertent actions of people, or external events (weather, disasters, war, etc.). Any of these sources of risk can affect both the acquirer directly and the external entities on which the acquirer depends.

Typical items addressed in an operational risk management plan include:

  • the scope of operational risk management activities
  • the methods to be used for operational risk identification, analysis, mitigation, monitoring, and communication
  • the sources of operational risk
  • how the sources of operational risk should be organized, categorized, compared, and consolidated
  • parameters for measuring and taking action on operational risks
  • risk mitigation techniques to be used, such as the development of layered administrative, technical, and physical controls
  • definition of risk measures to monitor the status of operational risks
  • time intervals for risk monitoring

Typical Work Products

  • Complete, written risk management plan

Criteria for Full Implementation Response

  • There is a documented plan for managing operational risks, and this document is used to guide risk management.

Criteria for Partial Implementation Response

  • The operational risk management plan is incomplete, or it exists but does not guide risk management in the organization, or the practice appears otherwise incomplete.
  • (Otherwise, the answer is marked as No Implementation)

Possible Evidence

  • Signatures included on a Risk Management Strategy or plan that covers supply chain risk management.

Reference to standards/source assessments

  • EDM: RF:G3.Q1
  • NIST 800-53, Rev. 5: SR-1, SR-2

Criteria for Partial Implementation Response

Possible Evidence

The knowledge gained through managing incidents can be used by the organization to improve the plan.

questions.title: WI:AE-1.Q2
questions.text: Is the baseline of network operations managed (reviewed and updated regularly)?
questions.supplemental:
Importance: System information exchanges include connections via leased lines or virtual private networks, connections to internet service providers, database sharing or exchanges of database transaction information, connections and exchanges with cloud services, exchanges via web-based services, or exchanges of files via file transfer protocols, network protocols (e.g., IPv4, IPv6), email, or other organization-to-organization communications. Organizations consider the risk related to new or increased threats that may be introduced when systems exchange information with other systems that may have different security and privacy requirements and controls.

Question Intent: To determine if the established baseline of network operations is managed for all systems and assets that support the critical service.

  • Baseline configurations are formally reviewed.
  • Maintaining baseline configurations requires creating new baselines as organizational information systems change over time.

Criteria for Full Implementation Response

  • The established baseline of network operations is managed for all systems and assets that support the critical service.

Criteria for Partial Implementation Response

Criteria for Partial Implementation Response
