questions.title: RE:CO-5.Q2
questions.text: Is relevant threat information communicated to the Incident Management Function?
questions.supplemental:
Importance: Organizations should communicate threat information to stakeholders, including the Incident Management Function.

Question Intent: To determine if threat information is communicated to all identified internal and external incident management personnel. The intent of communicating threat information is to assist incident handling and response personnel to perform their duties.

  • Threat information must be communicated according to established procedures.
  • Communication requirements may dictate that various communications methods and channels should be considered and identified.
  • Typical work products include:
  • threat communications to the incident handling team
  • threat communication standards and guidelines
  • standardized report templates
  • communication escalation protocols
  • list of incident management personnel and contact information
  • stakeholder communication requirements
  • documented methods and channels
  • tools and techniques for communication

Criteria for Full Implementation Response

  • Threat information is communicated to all identified incident handling and response personnel.

Criteria for Partial Implementation Response

  • Threat information is communicated to some of the identified incident management personnel.

Possible evidence

  • Threat communications to the incident handling team, threat communication standards and guidelines

Reference to standards/source assessments

  • NIST 800-53, Rev. 5: SI-5, PM-15

questions.title: RE:IM-1.Q2
questions.text: Are system incidents reviewed and lessons learned captured for future reference?
questions.supplemental:
Importance: It is important to develop these criteria with the stakeholders to ensure that post-incident reviews occur on all appropriate incidents, and do not consume unnecessary resources on those that do not meet the established thresholds.

Question Intent: To determine if there are documented criteria that guides the organization with determining which incidents require a post incident review.

  • This practice ensures that post-incident analysis meetings or reviews are held after significant incidents. The organization will use the criteria to help define “significant.”
  • The intent of these reviews is to identify any issues encountered or lessons learned, to propose areas for improvement, and to act on any findings or recommendations.

Examples of documented criteria:

  • departure from standard procedures
  • incidents of significant impact
  • incidents with unknown root cause
  • incidents of potential criminal activity
  • incidents of potential insider threat
  • incidents required by regulation to be reviewed

Criteria for Full Implementation Response

  • The organization uses documented criteria to evaluate all incidents for post incident review.

Criteria for Partial Implementation Response

  • The criteria for post-incident review is in development and partially documented.
  • Or, the criteria exist, but are used for only some incidents.

Possible evidence

  • A documented list of criteria for identifying incidents that require post-incident review.

Reference to standards/source assessments

  • IMR: PI:G1.Q1
  • NIST 800-53, Rev. 5: CP-2, IR-4, IR-8

questions.title: RE:IM-2.Q2
questions.text: Are response strategies reviewed and revised on a strictly defined period, at least annually?
questions.supplemental:
Importance: Review the plan to ensure that the organization is following the roadmap for maturing the capability and for fulfilling its incident response goals, incorporating lessons learned, addressing   organizational changes and problems encountered during plan implementation, execution, or testing.

Question Intent: To determine if the response strategy/plan is reviewed and updated on a strictly defined period (e.g., annually) as defined by the organization.

  • The knowledge gained through managing incidents can be used by the organization to improve the strategy/plan.
  • The plan review should include all relevant stakeholders to ensure proper coordination of requirements.
  • The date of the most recent review (even if no changes are necessary) should be annotated in the plan.
  • Details on how the plan is to be reviewed (periodicity, stakeholders, approving authority, etc.) should be documented in the plan or other governance documentation for the organization.
  • Review the plan to:
  • ensure that the organization is following the roadmap for maturing the capability and for fulfilling its incident response goals.
  • ensure that lessons learned from responding to incidents are also incorporated in the plan to improve the incident management process and life cycle.
  • ensure organizational changes are assessed, and the plan updated as necessary.
  • revise and update documented commitments from those responsible for implementing and supporting the plan, particularly the commitment of higher-level managers

Criteria for Full Implementation Response

  • The organization periodically reviews and updates the response plan/strategy on a strictly defined period.

Criteria for Partial Implementation Response

  • The organization has reviewed and updated the response plan/strategy but has not established a strictly defined frequency for the review.

Possible evidence

  • Minutes from response plan/strategy review meetings
  • Updated response plan/strategy containing updated details from past plan/strategy reviews.

Reference to standards/source assessments

  • Cyber IST: 10.2. C-IST Cybersecurity Plan.
  • IMR: PR:G1.Q2
  • NIST 800-53, Rev. 5: CP-2, IR-4, IR-8

questions.title: RE:MI-1.Q3
questions.text: Is analysis performed to ensure that the resolution is fully addressing the incident?
questions.supplemental:
Importance: Performing analysis on the incident resolution provides a mechanism for the organization to know that the incident has been fully addressed or if gaps continue to exist.

Question Intent: To verify that the incident resolution put in place fully addresses the incident.

Incident resolution analysis is done to determine if the incident has been fully addressed, identify any issues or gaps that may remain and act on any findings to fully address the incident.

Analysis may include:

  • a design review of the controls and other mechanisms put in place to address the incident and their ability to fully resolve it.
  • development and execution of tests that demonstrate the measures put in place actually resolve the incident.

Criteria for Full Implementation Response

  • The organization has analyzed all incident response measures put in place to resolve each incident and verify that each incident has been fully addressed.

Criteria for Partial Implementation Response

  • The organization has analyzed all incident response measures put in place for some incidents and verifies that some incidents have been fully addressed.

Possible evidence

  • Incident resolution analysis reports detailing the analysis approach, the results and how any gaps were addressed.

Reference to standards/source assessments

  •  NIST 800-53, Rev. 5: IR-4, IR-5, AU-6

questions.title: RE:MI-2.Q2
questions.text: Is the effectiveness of vulnerability mitigation reviewed?
questions.supplemental:
Importance: Review of the effectiveness of vulnerability mitigation plays an important role in both quality control of the vulnerability management process and in serving as a double-check on solutions.

Question Intent: To determine if the effectiveness of vulnerability mitigation is reviewed.

The organization should review mitigation activities to ensure they are effective in reducing or eliminating the exposure to identified vulnerabilities.

Criteria for Full Implementation Response

  • The organization reviews the effectiveness of all mitigating activities.

Criteria for “Incomplete” Response:

  • The organization reviews the effectiveness of some mitigating activities.

Possible evidence

  • Vulnerability management review documents

questions.title: RE:RD-2.Q2
questions.text: Does the organization maintain a supply of spare parts (i.e., system components) for critical systems?
questions.supplemental:
Importance: The availability and integrity of key system components are very important as their corruption or lack of availability could result in significant impact.  Techniques such as maintaining spare components where appropriate can prevent attacks from having mission or business level consequences.

Question Intent: To determine if the organization maintains a supply of spare parts (system components) for the critical service/HVA environment.

  • Maintain extra capacity, including spare parts where appropriate, for information storage, processing, or communications. Do not economize on resources; provide surge capacity.
  • Where possible, use diverse resources to provide surplus capacity (including spare system components).
  • Organizations should specify the system components that result in increased risk to organizational operations when the functionality provided by those components is not operational.
  • Provide substitute system components and a means to exchange active and standby components in accordance with policy and established processes.
  • Transferring primary system component responsibilities to other substitute components prior to primary component failure is important to reducing the risk of degraded or debilitated mission or business functions.

Criteria for Full Implementation Response

  • The organization maintains a supply of spare parts for all critical service/HVA system components identified by the organization as requiring spares.

Criteria for Partial Implementation Response

  • The organization maintains a supply of spare parts for some critical service/HVA system components identified by the organization as requiring spares.

Possible evidence

  • A documented list or inventory that indicates which system components require spares.
  • A documented inventory of the spare parts actually on hand and available for use.

Reference to standards/source assessments

  • NIST 800-160, Rev. 1 
  • NIST 800-53, Rev. 5: MA-6

questions.title: RE:RD-3.Q2
questions.text: Does the organization maintain a redundant secondary system that is not collocated with the primary system and that can be activated without loss of information or disruption to operations?
questions.supplemental:
Importance: The effect of system backup can be achieved and readily activated without loss of information or disruption to operations of the critical service/HVA environment.

Question Intent: To determine if the organization has implemented a backup solution that employs redundant systems or system components where the redundant system components are not collocated with the primary system and where they can be activated without loss of information or disruption to the operations of the critical service/HVA.

  • The effect of system backup can be achieved by maintaining a redundant secondary system that mirrors the primary system, including the replication of information.
  • The duplicated systems or system components are required to be in distributed locations.
  • The synchronization of duplicated and redundant services and data helps to ensure that information contained in the distributed locations can be used in the mission or business functions of organizations, as needed.
  • If this type of redundancy is in place and there is sufficient geographic separation between the two systems, the secondary system can also serve as the alternate processing site.

Criteria for Full Implementation Response

  • The organization has implemented redundant secondary system components that are not collocated with the primary system and can be readily activated without loss of information or disruption to the critical service/HVA operations.

Criteria for Partial Implementation Response

  • Redundant secondary system components that are not collocated with the primary system and can be readily activated without loss of information or disruption are in development and the configuration is partially documented.

Possible evidence

  • Documentation detailing the implementation and configuration of the redundant secondary system components.
  • Log files, directory folder file listings, and other related information showing the operation of the redundant system and system components.
  • Results from failover testing where the secondary becomes the primary environment.

Reference to standards/source assessments

  • NIST 800-53, Rev. 5: CP-9(6)

references.title: NIST SP 800-53 Rev. 5: Security and Privacy Controls for Information Systems and Organizations

questions.title: AD:IM-1.Q3
questions.text: Are test results compared with test objectives to identify needed improvements to recovery and service continuity plans?
questions.supplemental:
Importance: Comparison of implementation test results is used to identify gaps and track improvement of the service continuity plan over the life of a given system.

Question Intent: To determine if test results are compared to test objectives to identify improvements to recovery and service continuity plans. Improvements to the plans are driven by objective evaluation of the systems over time.

  • Regular testing and exercise of the service continuity plans: The objective of service continuity plan testing is to ensure that plans work as intended.
  • Testing identifies required improvements to the service continuity plans as well as the associated test plans.
  • The evaluation of test results involves comparing the documented test results against the established test objectives.
  • Areas where objectives could not be met are recorded, and strategies are developed to review and revise the plans.
  • Improvements to the testing process and plans should also be identified, documented, and incorporated into future tests.
  • Examples of clearly defined test objectives include: MTTR, RPO, RTO, etc.
  • Improvement Areas may include:
  • lack of sufficient resources
  • lack of appropriate resources
  • training gaps for plan staff and stakeholders
  • plan conflicts (if multiple plans are tested simultaneously)
  • required changes to infrastructure

Criteria for Full Implementation Response

  • Test results for each service continuity plan required for the delivery of the critical service are compared with test objectives to identify needed improvements.
  • The system will be considered to have fully addressed this question if established baselines, previous test result, and clear testing objectives are documented and used to improve the service continuity plans.

Criteria for Partial Implementation Response

  • Test results for some service continuity plans are compared with test objectives to identify needed improvements. (Otherwise, the answer is marked as No Implementation)

Possible Evidence

  • Documented test results, list of improvements to service continuity plans, list of improvements to service continuity test plans

Reference to standards/source assessments

  • CRR: SCM:G3.Q5
  • NIST 800-53, Rev. 5: IR-4, CP-2

references.title: NIST SP 800-53 Rev. 5: Security and Privacy Controls for Information Systems and Organizations
NIST SP 800-53 Rev. 5: Security and Privacy Controls for Information Systems and Organizations

questions.title: AD:CO-3.Q3
questions.text: Are the types and extent of communications needed by the organization to support stakeholders identified?
questions.supplemental:
Importance: Organizations must understand stakeholder needs if they are to write successful incident management and recovery communications plans. This detailed understanding will help organizations select appropriate method, frequency, and level of detail associated with communications.

Question Intent: The foundation for communications requirements is the needs of stakeholders. The variety of communication types and duration is directly related to the diversity of the stakeholder community. For example, an internal communication might be about general awareness or about a specific event or incident. External communications might be public relations messages, critical communications during a crisis, or the execution of a service continuity plan.

In addition to stakeholders, communications requirements may also be derived directly from the needs of other operational resilience management processes. For example, the ways in which the organization must distribute information collected in the monitoring process may create requirements that must be met by the communications process.

The organization must establish communications requirements as the foundation for the development and execution of a communications plan to support incident management and recovery activities. Requirements help the organization to determine the scope of the communications process, plan, and program and to ensure the development of appropriate and cost-effective delivery mechanisms and infrastructure to support communications needs. Requirements determine whether communications methods are:

  • oral or written, or both
  • provided on a one-time basis, at regular intervals, on an ongoing basis, or on demand
  • provided on media that are disposable or able to be archived
  • provided on more than one media type (paper, electronic, etc.)

Communications requirements also provide the foundation for the development and implementation of an infrastructure (people, processes, and technology) to support all types of resilience communication.

Criteria for Full Implementation Response

  • All stakeholder incident response and recovery communications needs are identified.

Criteria for Partial Implementation Response

  • Some stakeholder incident response and recovery communications needs are identified conditions constitutes an Incomplete. (Otherwise, the answer is marked as No Implementation)

Possible Evidence

  • Communications requirements by stakeholder and process

Reference to standards/source assessments

  • CERT RMM COMM:SG1.SP2
  • NIST 800-53, Rev. 5: CP-2, IR-4

references.title: NIST SP 800-53 Rev. 5: Security and Privacy Controls for Information Systems and Organizations
NIST SP 800-53 Rev. 5: Security and Privacy Controls for Information Systems and Organizations

questions.title: AD:RL-1.Q3
questions.text: Does the organization analyze systems or system components to ensure that system resources are being used consistent with their intended purpose?
questions.supplemental:
Importance: Ensuring that cyber resources are used consistently with mission or business function purposes and approved uses will help avoid mission/scope creep which can increase a system’s attack surface.

Question Intent: To determine if there is an implemented process to analyze system components and ensure that the information resources are being used consistent with their intended purpose.

  • Ensure that cyber resources are used consistently with mission or business function purposes and approved uses. Avoid “mission creep,” which can increase a system’s attack surface.
  • Systems are designed to support a specific mission or business function. However, over time, systems and system components may be used to support services and functions that are outside of the scope of the intended mission or business functions.
  • This mission or scope creep can result in exposing information resources to unintended environments and uses that can significantly increase threat exposure.
  • Exposing information resources to unintended environments and uses may make the systems more vulnerable to compromise, which can ultimately impact the services and functions for which they were intended.
  • By analyzing information resource use, organizations can identify such potential exposures.

Criteria for Full Implementation Response

  • A process to analyze critical service/HVA system components to ensure all information resources are being used consistent with their intended purpose has been implemented and documented.
  • As part of the Assessment & Authorization (A&A) process or an Ongoing Authorization process, system components are analyzed to ensure that they are being used consistent with their intended mission/business purpose(s).

Criteria for Partial Implementation Response

  • A process to analyze critical service/HVA system components to ensure all information resources are being used consistent with their intended purpose is in development and partially documented.

Possible Evidence

  • A documented process to analyze critical service/HVA system components to ensure all information resources are being used consistent with their intended purpose.
  • Documented outcomes of the process detailing analysis and the associated results.

Reference to standards/source assessments

  • NIST 800-53, Rev. 5: PM-32

references.title: NIST SP 800-53 Rev. 5: Security and Privacy Controls for Information Systems and Organizations

questions.title: AD:RL-2.Q3
questions.text: Does the organization outsource nonessential services to a managed service provider?
questions.supplemental:
Importance: Maintaining all functions on the same primary systems or system components increases the attack surface of the organization’s mission-essential functions or services.

Question Intent: To determine if the organization offloads or outsources service or system functions  to a managed service provider.

  • Offload functions to other systems or to an external provider that is better able to perform the functions securely
  • Offloading reduces the attack surface and motivates ongoing consideration of what is essential.
  • Not every function or service that a system provides is essential to the organizational mission or business functions. General printing or copying is an example of a non-essential but supporting service for an organization.
  • Whenever feasible, such supportive but non-essential functions or services are not co-located with the functions or services that support essential mission or business functions.
  • Maintaining nonessential functions on the same system or system component increases the attack surface of the organization’s mission-essential functions or services.
  • Moving supportive but non-essential functions to a non-critical system, system component, or external provider can also increase efficiency by putting those functions or services under the control of individuals or providers who are subject matter experts in the functions or services.

Criteria for Full Implementation Response

  • The organization has determined which functions or services are considered nonessential.
     AND
  • The organization has outsourced all of the applicable nonessential functions or services to a managed service provider.

Criteria for Partial Implementation Response

  • The organization is in the process of determining which functions or services are considered nonessential.
  • Or, the organization has determined which functions or services are considered nonessential and is in the process of outsourcing all of the applicable nonessential functions or services to a managed service provider.

Possible Evidence

  • A documented list of which functions or services the organization has determined to be nonessential
  • An agreement with a managed service provider showing their management of the applicable nonessential functions or services.

Reference to standards/source assessments

  • NIST 800-53, Rev. 5: PM-7(1)

references.title: NIST SP 800-53 Rev. 5: Security and Privacy Controls for Information Systems and Organizations

questions.title: AD:RL-3.Q3
questions.text: Does the organization implement its risk management process for any vulnerabilities identified during attack surface reviews?
questions.supplemental:
Importance: Managing the vulnerabilities identified during the attack surface reviews will reduce risk to organizations by giving attackers less opportunity to exploit weaknesses or deficiencies.

Question Intent: To determine if the organization employs its risk management process to manage to closure the vulnerabilities identified during the attack surface reviews.

  • Attack surface reduction is closely aligned with threat and vulnerability analyses and system architecture and design.
  • Attack surface reduction is a means of reducing risk to organizations by giving attackers less opportunity to exploit weaknesses or deficiencies (i.e., potential vulnerabilities) within systems, system components, and system services.
  • Attack surface reduction includes:
  • implementing the concept of layered defenses,
  • applying the principles of least privilege and least functionality,
  • applying secure software development practices,
  • deprecating unsafe functions,
  • reducing entry points available to unauthorized users,
  • reducing the amount of code that executes,
  • and eliminating application programming interfaces (APIs) that are vulnerable to attacks.

Criteria for Full Implementation Response

  • The organization employs its risk management process (or other similar process) to manage to closure all vulnerabilities identified during the attack surface reviews of the critical service/HVA environment.

Criteria for Partial Implementation Response

  • The organization employs its risk management process (or other similar process) to manage to closure some vulnerabilities identified during the attack surface reviews of the critical service/HVA environment.

Possible Evidence

  • Documentation detailing the implementation of the risk management process and its application to managing the vulnerabilities identified during attack surface reviews including the results of the process. This may be presented in the form of a report or other tracking mechanism.

Reference to standards/source assessments:

  • NIST 800-53, Rev. 5: SA-15(5), SA-15(7)

questions.title: AN:AR-1.Q3
questions.text: Does the organization use threat intelligence and other sources to inform its operating configurations?
questions.supplemental:
Importance: Threat intelligence, or other external sources, may be employed to assist in performing reconfiguration based on current relevant threats to the system.

Question Intent: Determine if the organization is incorporating the latest industry relevant source data into its reconfiguration plan.

Criteria for Full Implementation Response

  • The organization utilizes at least one automatically updating threat intelligence source that is tailored to the target system(s).

Criteria for Partial Implementation Response

  • The organization utilizes threat intelligence data on an irregular schedule or without tailoring to the target system(s).

Possible Evidence

  • Configuration Management Plan, System Security Plans

Reference to standards/source assessments

  • NIST 800-53, Rev. 5: CM-6(1), PM-16(1)

questions.title: AN:AR-2.Q3
questions.text: Describe the SOC's process for prioritizing incident response activities. (Select one)
questions.supplemental:
Importance: Prioritization of events determine the application of resources. Application of resources influences outcomes.

Question Intent: Determine what the SOC’s, if present, procedure for prioritizing incidents.

Criteria for Full Implementation Response

  • There is an SOC with a clear and written incident response policy that includes prioritization guidance.

Criteria for Partial Implementation Response

  • There is generic guidance that informs an ad hoc decision concerning the prioritization of incident response activities.

Possible Evidence

  • Incident Response Plan, System Security Plans

Reference to standards/source assessments

  • NIST 800-53, Rev. 5: IR-6

options.text: Formal written incident response policy that includes prioritization guidance
A manager determines priorities and allocates resources
Incident response prioritization is ad hoc
The organization addresses incidents on a first-come, first-served basis

questions.title: AN:AR-3.Q3
questions.text: Do you employ security solutions that leverage artificial intelligence or machine learning (as opposed to a signature-based capability) that can respond dynamically to attacks or anomalous activity?
questions.supplemental:
Importance: Artificial intelligence/machine learning solutions may provide more comprehensive information system and network protection from evolving attack vectors.

Question Intent: Determine if the system utilizes responsive AI and/or ML in its defensive capabilities.

Criteria for Full Implementation Response

  • The organization does utilize some form of AI/ML for system that is capable of automatically responding to identified threats.

Criteria for Partial Implementation Response

  • The system utilizes AI/ML for system monitoring/logging, but that capability has no ability to respond to identified attacks or anomalous activity.

Possible Evidence

  • Runbooks or configuration files for network devices, specific implementation details in a System Security Plan (SSP).

Reference to standards/source assessments

  • NIST 800-53, Rev. 5: RA-3(4)

questions.title: AN:BE-3.Q3
questions.text: Are the organization's mission, objectives, and activities prioritized?
questions.supplemental:
Importance: Prioritization of organizational objectives and activities will help prioritize the assets and services supporting these. The high-value services that support strategic objectives should be prioritized as the focus of resilience activities. 

Question Intent: Determine if the organization prioritizes its mission, objectives, and activities. 

Criteria for Full Implementation Response

  • The organization has categorized its objectives and supporting activities into different priorities – or at least higher priority than other less essential objectives and activities. 

Criteria for Partial Implementation Response

  • Only objectives or only activities but not both are prioritized.

Possible Evidence

  • Prioritized list of high-value services, list of prioritized objectives, list of prioritized activities. 

Reference to standards/source assessments

  • NIST 800-53, Rev. 5: RA-2(1), PM-11
  • CRR: AM:G1.Q4
  • CERT RMM EF:SG1.SP3

questions.title: AN:BE-4.Q3
questions.text: Is the prioritization of assets reviewed and validated?
questions.supplemental:
Importance: The asset list should be reviewed and validated periodically to ensure it remains valid/current.

Question Intent: Determine if prioritization of assets is reviewed and validated periodically and how recent was the most recent review. 

Criteria for Full Implementation Response

  • There is a prioritized list of assets that has been reviewed and validated annually.

Criteria for Partial Implementation Response

  • There is a prioritized list of assets, but it does not seem to link facilities to priority services, or
  • There is a prioritized list of assets, but it has not been reviewed in over 12 months. 

Possible Evidence

  • List of high-value assets with date (history) of reviews.

  • CRR: AM:G7.Q2

questions.text: Have resilience requirements of the critical service been established that apply specifically to each external dependency?
questions.supplemental:
Importance: Critical services may have external dependencies with associated resilience requirements.

Question Intent: Determine if resilience requirements of the critical service been established that apply specifically to each external dependency

  • Documented resilience requirements for each external dependency and associated service level agreements

Criteria for Partial Implementation Response

  • Having partial (over 40% but less than 75%) SLAs and resilience requirements

  • Documented resilience requirements for each external dependency, Service level agreements

questions.title: AN:CA-2.Q3
questions.text: Does the organization maintain a mission-wide or organization-wide operational picture or dashboard?
questions.supplemental:
Importance: The organization’s ability to maintain a single, identical display of information facilitates the planning and execution of operational and security activities.

Question Intent: Does the organization maintain a mission-wide or organization-wide operational picture or dashboard that displays operational and security event or incidents? Does this “Common Operational Picture” support risk management and decision-making?

  • Definition of any key words with examples

Common Operational Picture (COP): A single, identical display of relevant information shared by more than one [organizational unit] that facilitates collaborative planning and assists all echelons to achieve situational awareness.

Criteria for Full Implementation Response

  • The organization maintains a mission-wide or organization-wide operational picture or dashboard that is monitored by dedicated personnel.

Criteria for Partial Implementation Response

  • The organization maintains multiple operational pictures or dashboards. Collectively, the operational pictures or dashboard provide mission-wide or enterprise-wide coverage.
  • The organization maintains a mission-wide operational picture or dashboard, but it is not monitored by dedicated personnel.
  • (Otherwise, the answer is marked as No Implementation)

Possible Evidence

  • Screenshots of the organization-wide operational picture or dashboard

Reference to standards/source assessments

  • NIST 800-53, Rev. 5: IR-4(14)

references.title: NIST SP 800-53 Rev. 5: Security and Privacy Controls for Information Systems and Organizations

questions.title: AN:CP-1.Q3
questions.text: Are multiple, distinct authentication challenges over the course of a session employed to confirm identity?
questions.supplemental:
Importance: Multifactor authentication that employs multiple authentication mechanisms can prevent against attacks that leverage legitimate user credentials. By having multiple distinct authentication challenges that incorporate passphrases, biometrics, physical tokens, or SMS passcodes, organizations can make it significantly more difficult for adversaries to access user accounts.

Question Intent: This question seeks to discover what authentication challenges are employed over the course of a user session and determine whether multifactor authentication is in use.

Multifactor authentication uses two or more different factors to achieve authentication. Factors include something you know (e.g., PIN, password), something you have (e.g., cryptographic identification device, token), or something you are (e.g., biometric).

Criteria for Full Implementation Response

  • The organization demonstrates that a minimum of two distinct authentication challenges are employed when initiating a user session.

Criteria for Partial Implementation Response

  • The organization uses less than two authentication challenges or cannot provide input regarding specific details of the implementation.
  • (Otherwise, the answer is marked as No Implementation)

Possible Evidence

  • Standard operating procedures regarding authentication processes, screenshots from a user’s point-of-view demonstrating a requirement to complete multiple distinct authentication challenges while establishing a session, screenshots from an administrator’s point of view showing that multi-factor authentication is enabled.

Reference to standards/source assessments

  • NIST 800-53, Rev. 5: RA-2
  • NIST 800-160, Rev. 1

references.title: NIST SP 800-53 Rev. 5: Security and Privacy Controls for Information Systems and Organizations

questions.title: AN:CP-2.Q3
questions.text: Does the organization employ privilege analysis tools and/or methods to support an ongoing review of whether user privileges are assigned consistently?
questions.supplemental:
Importance: Periodic recertification of privileged accounts is an important task to ensure that users are allocated privileges commensurate with their job duties and to ensure that the principle of least privilege is implemented at the system level.

Question Intent: This question ascertains if the organization uses privilege analysis tools to support an ongoing review of whether user privileges are assigned consistently.

Criteria for Full Implementation Response

  • The organization utilizes privilege analysis tools that can support a continuous review of user privileges and how they are assigned across the organization.

Criteria for Partial Implementation Response

  • The organization uses privilege analysis tools to support the review of user account privileges. However, the tools might not have capabilities to discern whether user privileges are assigned consistently across the organization.
  • (Otherwise, the answer is marked as No Implementation)

Possible Evidence

  • Account management standard operating procedures, policy for user account provisioning.

Reference to standards/source assessments

  • NIST 800-53, Rev. 5: CP-2(1)

references.title: NIST SP 800-53 Rev. 5: Security and Privacy Controls for Information Systems and Organizations

questions.title: AN:CP-3.Q3
questions.text: Does the incident management plan identify sub-classes of incidents that require defined responses to ensure continuation of mission and business functions?
questions.supplemental:
Importance: Certain incidents can cause significant amounts of destruction or disruption to business functions. Therefore, organizations should identify these incidents and document them in an incident management plan.

Question Intent: If the incident management plan includes classes of incidents that require specific responses to ensure the continuation of mission-critical business functions.

Classes of incidents include malfunctions due to design or implementation errors and omissions, targeted malicious attacks, and untargeted malicious attacks. Incident response actions include orderly system degradation, system shutdown, fall back to manual mode or activation of alternative technology whereby the system operates differently, employing deceptive measures, alternate information flows, or operating in a mode that is reserved for when systems are under attack. 

Criteria for Full Implementation Response

  • The organization fully documents sub-classes of incidents and actions to take in response to such incidents to ensure continuation of organizational missions and business functions.

Criteria for Partial Implementation Response

  • The organization partially documents sub-classes of incidents and actions to take in response to such incidents to ensure continuation of organizational missions and business functions.
  • (Otherwise, the answer is marked as No Implementation)

Possible Evidence

  • Sub-classes of incidents and their corresponding actions as defined in the organizational incident management plan.

Reference to standards/source assessments

  • NIST 800-53, Rev. 5: IR-4(3)

references.title: NIST SP 800-53 Rev. 5: Security and Privacy Controls for Information Systems and Organizations

questions.title: AN:CP-4.Q3
questions.text: Does the organization employ an independent penetration testing agent or team to perform penetration testing on the system or system components?
questions.supplemental:
Importance: Using an independent team or external firm specializing in penetration tests can provide additional perspectives to the engagement and create a more effective adversary emulation if the organization is seeking to mimic an attack from a competent, sophisticated adversary--I.e., an attack advanced persistent threat group.

Question Intent: This question discerns what party or entity is responsible for the performance of penetration testing against organizational systems or system components.

Having penetration tests being performed by an independent testing agent has their limitations in the reporting as you’re limited to the toolkit and skillset of a single penetration tester, however this may be more cost effective depending on the size and scope of the penetration testing engagement desired.

Additional factors such as whether the penetration tester is an employee of the organization can also determine the kind of testing exercise able to be performed, while organizational personnel may be capable of performing a “white box” pen test, they would not fully be able to perform a “black box” test due to their familiarity and knowledge of the organization.

This may be a justification for external penetration testing services, to get an honest look at what is visible to outsiders.

If seeking to emulate an insider threat, there are benefits to using penetration testers with knowledge of the organization.

Criteria for Full Implementation Response

  • The organization employs an independent penetration testing agent or teams to perform penetration testing on organizational systems or system components.

Criteria for Partial Implementation Response

  • The organization employs an independent penetration testing agent or teams to perform penetration testing on some organizational systems or system components, but not all.
  • (Otherwise, the answer is marked as No Implementation)

Possible Evidence

  • Copy of a penetration testing report / write up authored by an independent penetration testing agent or team.

Reference to standards/source assessments

  • NIST 800-53, Rev. 5: CA-8(1)

references.title: NIST SP 800-53 Rev. 5: Security and Privacy Controls for Information Systems and Organizations

questions.title: AN:DI-2.Q3
questions.text: Does the organization implement out-of-band authentication mechanisms under organization-defined conditions?
questions.supplemental:
Importance: Out-of-band authentication can be used to provide increased levels of security. For example, out-of-band authentication can be used to mitigate actual or suspected man-in the-middle attacks. 

Question Intent: This question determines if the organization implements out-of-band authentication mechanisms to authenticate users or devices to an information system. 

Out-of-band authentication refers to the use of two separate communication paths to identify and authenticate users or devices to an information system. 

The first path (i.e., the in-band path) is used to identify and authenticate users or devices and is generally the path through which information flows. The second path (i.e., the out-of-band path) is used to independently verify the authentication and/or requested action. 

For example, a user authenticates via a notebook computer to a remote server to which the user desires access and requests some action of the server via that communication path. Subsequently, the server contacts the user via the user’s cell phone to verify that the requested action originated from the user. The user may confirm the intended action to an individual on the telephone or provide an authentication code via the telephone. 

Criteria for Full Implementation Response

  • The organization implements out-of-band authentication mechanisms to authenticate users or devices to all designated critical service assets or high value information system assets as appropriate.

Criteria for Partial Implementation Response

  • The organization implements out-of-band authentication mechanisms to authenticate users or devices to some designated critical service assets or high value information system assets as appropriate.

Possible Evidence

  • Configuration documentation detailing the out-of-band authentication mechanisms setup and showing that it is in place and used for controlling access.

Reference to standards/source assessments

  • NIST 800-53, Rev. 5: IA-2(13)

references.title: NIST SP 800-53 Rev. 5: Security and Privacy Controls for Information Systems and Organizations

questions.title: AN:DI-3.Q3
questions.text: Does the organization take measures to limit harm from potential adversaries identifying and targeting the organizational supply chain?
questions.supplemental:
Importance: Weaknesses or deficiencies in supply chain elements or processes represent potential vulnerabilities that can be exploited by adversaries to cause harm to the organization and affect its ability to carry out its core missions or business functions. 

Question Intent: This question determines if the organization takes measures or implements controls to limit the harm from the organization’s supply chain. 

Controls that can be implemented to reduce the probability of adversaries successfully identifying and targeting the supply chain include:

  • avoiding the purchase of custom or non-standardized configurations, 
  • employing approved vendor lists with standing reputations in industry 
  • following pre-agreed maintenance schedules and update and patch delivery mechanisms,
  • maintaining a contingency plan in case of a supply chain event, 
  • using procurement carve-outs that provide exclusions to commitments or obligations, 
  • using diverse delivery routes, 
  • minimizing the time between purchase decisions and delivery. 

Criteria for Full Implementation Response

  • The organization has documented and implemented measures (controls) to limit harm from the organization’s supply chain.

Criteria for Partial Implementation Response

  • The organization has documented and implemented some measures (controls) to limit harm from the organization’s supply chain.

Possible Evidence

  • A list of supply chain related controls and associated documentation or configuration information.

Reference to standards/source assessments

  • NIST 800-53, Rev. 5: SR-3(2)

references.title: NIST SP 800-53 Rev. 5: Security and Privacy Controls for Information Systems and Organizations

questions.title: AN:GV-1.Q3
questions.text: Is there a documented policy for change management?
questions.supplemental:
Importance: Organizations should have a documented policy for change management as it establishes the organizational expectations for planning and performing the change management process as well as communicates those expectations to the organization.

Question Intent: This question determines if a policy for performing change management activities exists.

A policy is a written communication from the organization’s senior management to employees.

The change management policy should address:

  • responsibility, authority, ownership, and the requirement to perform change management activities
  • establishment of procedures, standards, and guidelines
  • Requesting and approving changes to assets
  • measuring adherence to policy, exceptions granted, and policy violations
  • compliance with legal, regulatory, contractual, and government obligations

Criteria for Full Implementation Response

  • The organization has a documented policy for performing change management.

Criteria for Partial Implementation Response

  • A policy is in development and partially documented
  • (Otherwise, the answer is marked as No Implementation)

Possible Evidence

  • A Standard Operating Procedure for Change Management or Other relevant organizational policy covering change management.

Reference to standards/source assessments

  • CRR: CCM:MIL2.Q2
  • NIST 800-53, Rev. 5: CM-1

references.title: NIST SP 800-53 Rev. 5: Security and Privacy Controls for Information Systems and Organizations

questions.title: AN:GV-1.Q21
questions.text: Does the organization have a policy that requires periodic (at least annual) operational exercises of resilience functions?
questions.supplemental:
Importance: Operational exercises to test the effectiveness of organizational policy and procedures should be conducted at least annually.

questions.title: AN:GV-3.Q3
questions.text: Have requirements (rules, laws, regulations, policies, etc.) for identifying event evidence for forensic purposes been identified?
questions.supplemental:
Importance: Failure to comply with statutory requirements for evidence identification and classification can result in legal ramifications. Therefore, it is critical that organizations abide by the industry-specific, national, regional, and state regulations for the areas in which the organization operates.

Question Intent: This question determines if requirements for identifying event evidence for forensic purposes have been identified.

An event may become an organizational incident that has the potential to be a violation of local, state, or federal rules, laws, and regulations. For example:

  • Securities and Exchange Commission regulatory requirements
  • state privacy laws
  • Food and Drug Administration regulatory requirements
  • chain of custody requirements

This is often not known early in the investigation of an event, so the organization should ensure that all event evidence is handled properly

Criteria for Full Implementation Response

  • The organization has identified and documented relevant requirements for identifying event evidence for forensic purposes.

Criteria for Partial Implementation Response

  • Requirements for identifying event evidence are in development and partially documented.
  • (Otherwise, the answer is marked as No Implementation)

Possible Evidence

  • Incident response plan, Standard Operating Procedure for Incident Management, or Other relevant organizational policy covering incident management.

questions.title: AN:RM-1.Q3
questions.text: Has a plan for managing operational risk been agreed to by stakeholders?
questions.supplemental:
Importance: An operational risk management plan provides a common foundation for the performance of risk management activities. For External Dependencies Management, having a plan that includes external dependencies helps to coordinate management of these risks with the acquirer’s risk appetite and broader risk strategy.

Question Intent: This question determines if the organization has a plan for managing operational risk.

Operational risk is defined as the potential impact on assets and their related services that could result from inadequate or failed internal processes, failures of systems or technology, deliberate or inadvertent actions of people, or external events (weather, disasters, war, etc.). Any of these sources of risk can affect both the acquirer directly and the external entities on which the acquirer depends.

Typical items addressed in an operational risk management plan include:

  • the scope of operational risk management activities
  • the methods to be used for operational risk identification, analysis, mitigation, monitoring, and communication
  • the sources of operational risk
  • how the sources of operational risk should be organized, categorized, compared, and consolidated
  • parameters for measuring and taking action on operational risks
  • risk mitigation techniques to be used, such as the development of layered administrative, technical, and physical controls
  • definition of risk measures to monitor the status of operational risks
  • time intervals for risk monitoring and reassessment

Criteria for Full Implementation Response

  • There is a documented plan for managing operational risks, and this document is used to guide risk management.
  • The plan for managing operational risks has been approved by appropriate stakeholders.

Criteria for Partial Implementation Response

  • The operational risk management plan is incomplete or in draft, or it exists but does not guide risk management in the organization, or the plan hasn’t been approved by appropriate stakeholders, or the practice appears otherwise incomplete.
  • (Otherwise, the answer is marked as No Implementation)

Possible Evidence

  •  Complete, written risk management plan

Reference to standards/source assessments

  • EDM: RF:G3.Q1
  • NIST 800-53, Rev. 5: SA-2, PM-3, PM-7, PM-9, PM-10, PM-11

questions.title: AN:SC-1.Q3
questions.text: Does the acquirer have an established process for entering into formal agreements with external entities?
questions.supplemental:
Importance: Organizations should have a standardizes and consistent process established for entering into agreements with external entities.

Question Intent: This question determines if the acquirer has an established process for selecting and forming relationships with external entities that support the critical service.

Having an established process can help the acquirer make better selections, including choosing external entities that align more closely with the acquirer’s needs and requirements.

Having an established process means that:

  • There are specific steps or activities that acquirer staff must complete when completing the activity, in this case forming relationships on behalf of the acquirer.
  • The process is supported by documentation. The process need not be documented in one consolidated plan, but it should be documented to support the process. For example, staff responsible for sourcing suppliers may have written criteria for selecting suppliers. Staff may have a written checklist or other guidance to complete before submitting contracts for approval, etc.
  • The acquirer’s staff is aware that the process exists, and they are expected to follow it.
  • The process applies to formal agreements with type of external entity to support the critical service.

Typical Work Products

  • documented external entity selection criteria
  • roles and assignments of responsibility in job descriptions
  • internal reporting requirements
  • documented acquirer approval authorities
  • standard contract requirements

Criteria for Full Implementation Response

  • The acquirer has an established process for entering into formal agreements with external entities that support the critical service.

Criteria for Partial Implementation Response

  • Process exists but some staff are not aware of it, or it is not supported by documentation, or it applies only to some types of external entities, or the practice appears otherwise incomplete.
  • (Otherwise, the answer is marked as No Implementation)

Possible Evidence

  • Documentation that describes the process by which the organization enters into formal agreements with external entities.

Reference to standards/source assessments

  • NIST 800-53, Rev. 5: SA-9, SR-5(2)

questions.title: WI:AE-3.Q3
questions.text: Does the length of time that each identified audit log (including archives) is retained meet its documented retention requirements?

Importance: Storing audit records in a central repository separate from the audited system or system component helps to ensure that a compromise of the system being audited does not also result in a compromise of the audit records. Organizations may have multiple audit log storage repositories distributed across multiple system components with each repository having different storage volume capacities.

Question Intent: To determine if the length of time that each identified audit log (including archives) is retained meets its documented retention requirements.

Criteria for Partial Implementation Response

  • Or, all identified audit logs are retained but a retention period has not been documented for each log.

  • Policy for storing logs
  • List of recently deleted logs from central repository with dates

questions.title: WI:AM-1.Q3
questions.text: Have change criteria been established for asset descriptions?
questions.supplemental:
Importance: The organization should have a set of criteria to identify when changes to assets affect the delivery of the critical service and require a change to the asset description.

Question Intent: To determine if change criteria have been established for asset descriptions.

  • Change criteria should be applied consistently across all asset types.

Examples of criteria or triggers that can affect high-value assets:

  • Changes in services affecting the assets on which they rely (e.g., changes in availability requirements)
  • Changes in technology infrastructure and configuration
  • Creation or alteration of information
  • Contracts that the organization enters into that would identify new assets
  • Changes in organizational structure and staff—termination or transfer of staff between organizational units or changes in roles and responsibilities
  • Real-estate transactions that add, alter, or change existing facilities
  • Acquisition of assets such as technology or facilities

At a minimum, all high-value assets should be described and defined to the extent possible. Differences in the level of description are expected from asset to asset, and an organization must decide how much information is useful in facilitating requirements definition and satisfaction. The description of the asset should detail why it is considered to be of high value to the organization. There are some common elements that should be collected, at a minimum, for each asset.

These are examples of information that should be collected and documented for assets:

  • Asset type (people, information, technology, or facilities)
  • Categorization of asset by sensitivity (generally for information assets only)
  • Asset location (typically where the custodian is managing the asset)
  • Asset owners and custodians (particularly where this is external to the organization)
  • The format or form of the asset (particularly for information assets that might exist on paper and electronically)
  • Location where backups or duplicates of this asset exist (particularly for information assets)
  • The services that are dependent on the asset (See ADM:SG2.)
  • The value of the asset in either qualitative or quantitative terms
  • The asset’s resilience requirements

Criteria for Full Implementation Response

  • The organization has established asset description change criteria for all assets that support the critical service.

Criteria for Partial Implementation Response

  • The organization has established asset description change criteria for some assets.
  • (Otherwise, the answer is marked as No Implementation)

Possible evidence:

  • Documented list of asset description change criteria or triggers 

Reference to standards/source assessments

  • CRR: AM:G4.Q1-PITF
  • CERT RMM ADM:SG3.SP1
  • NIST 800-53, Rev. 5: CM-8, CM-8(1), PM-5

questions.title: WI:DE-1.Q3
questions.text: Does the organization remove, mask, encrypt, hash, or replace direct identifiers in a dataset?
questions.supplemental:
Importance: Removing identifiers improves privacy protection since information that is removed cannot be inadvertently disclosed or improperly used. Organizations may be subject to specific de-identification definitions or methods under applicable laws, regulations, or policies.

Question Intent: To determine if the organization removes, masks, encrypts, hashes, or replaces direct identifiers in relevant critical service/HVA datasets.

De-identification is the general term for the process of removing the association between a set of identifying data and the data subject. Many datasets contain information about individuals that can be used to distinguish or trace an individual’s identity, such as name, social security number, date and place of birth, mother’s maiden name, or biometric records.

There are many possible processes for removing direct identifiers from a dataset.

  • Columns in a dataset that contain a direct identifier can be removed.
  • In masking, the direct identifier is transformed into a repeating character, such as XXXXXX or 999999.
  • Identifiers can be encrypted or hashed so that the linked records remain linked.
  • In the case of encryption or hashing, algorithms are employed that require the use of a key, including the Advanced Encryption Standard or a Hash-based Message Authentication Code.
  • Identifiers can alternatively be replaced with a keyword, including transforming George Washington to PATIENT or replacing it with a surrogate value, such as transforming George Washington to Abraham Polk.

Criteria for Full Implementation Response

  • For all relevant critical service/HVA datasets, direct identifiers are removed, masked, encrypted, hashed, or replaced.

Criteria for Partial Implementation Response

  • For some relevant critical service/HVA datasets, direct identifiers are removed, masked, encrypted, hashed, or replaced

Possible evidence:

  • Relevant datasets that have had their direct identifiers altered.

Reference to standards/source assessments

questions.title: WI:DP-1.Q3
questions.text: Do all users receive training in how to recognize and report potential security events?
questions.supplemental:
Importance: Organizations must train their employees on how to recognize and report potential security events. That way in case detection mechanisms fail to identify security events, there are additional trained personnel embedded throughout the organization capable of detecting and reporting potential security events.

Question Intent: This question seeks to determine if employees are trained on how to recognize and report potential security events. Understanding what kinds of security events to look for as well as the appropriate channels to report to are critical topics that should be covered in security training within an organization.

Criteria for Full Implementation Response

  • Employees receive standard training in how to recognize and report potential security events. The organization can also show that employees are confident in utilizing reporting channels when necessary.

Criteria for Partial Implementation Response

  • The organization provides partial training on how to recognize and report potential security events, however the training is not consistently administered across the organization.
  • (Otherwise, the answer is marked as No Implementation)

Possible evidence

questions.title: WI:AC-1.Q3
questions.text: How quickly does the organization suspend or modify user accounts upon change of employment status (e.g., firing or layoff) or role (e.g., promotion or transfer)? (Select one)
questions.supplemental:
Importance: It is essential for an organization to update users’ access promptly to ensure that a user to not employ out-of-date permissions to access, modify, or delete materials without authorization.

Question Intent: Does the organization have a protocol for removing, suspending or modifying user accounts upon change of employment?

  • Following an adverse human resources action, when is an account modified, deleted, or de-activated? (I.e., fired, quits (bad terms)?
  • When a user leaves the organization, when is an account modified, deleted, or de-activated? (i.e., lay off, quits (“good” terms)?
  • When a user transfers into a new role, when is the account modified? This can include either an increase/decrease in user privileges, a move to a new organizational group, etc.
  • Does the organization test the account modification, deletion, and/or de-activation process as part of its security assessments and evaluations? Is a verification done to ensure that John Doe was removed completely?

Criteria for Full Implementation Response

  • The organization modifies accounts of all users on the same day as a change in employment status or role.

Criteria for Partial Implementation Response

  • The organization modifies accounts of some users on the same day as a change in employment status or role or of all users no later than one business day after the event.
  • (Otherwise, the answer is marked as No Implementation)

Possible evidence

  • Change management requests
  • Human resources change-in-status notifications/tickets

Reference to standards/source assessments

  • Cyber IST: Q.16.8

questions.title: WI:AC-2.Q3
questions.text: What controls are used to manage privileged accounts (to include contractors performing administrative functions)? (Select all that apply)
questions.supplemental:
Importance: Privileged accounts can provide attackers with heightened access to systems and the ability to cover their tracks to make detection more difficult. Increasing the security on such accounts is an important component to preventing their misuse.

Question Intent: To determine whether the organization employs additional security measures to prevent the misuse of privileged accounts, and to more rapidly detect that misuse when it occurs.

The security measures in the selection list address several different approaches to improving security on privileged accounts:

  • Reducing the total number of such accounts by creating them on a temporary basis.
  • Requiring dual authorization to reduce the likelihood that an individual can create a privileged account without management approval.
  • Increased training.
  • Enhanced logging and review of privileged activities.

All measures must be selected for an organization to be considered as implementing this control fully. Note that a Privileged Access Management solution may incorporate all of the required controls into a single product.

Criteria for Full Implementation Response

  • All items except “None of the above” are checked.

Criteria for Partial Implementation Response

  • Two to three items except “None of the above” are checked.
  • (Otherwise, the answer is marked as No Implementation)

Possible evidence

  • Training attendance or examination records
  • Human Resources records defining access requirements
  • Privileged account access issuance documentation
  • Records of review of audit logs

Reference to standards/source assessments

  • Cyber IST: Q.16.3
  • NIST 800-53, Rev. 5: AC-1, AC-2, AC-3, AC-5, AC-6, AC-14, AC-16, AC-24

All user accounts with administrator privileges require dual authorization.
All users with administrator privileges are trained on cybersecurity requirements.
All accounts with administrative level access are centrally logged and audited.

questions.title: WI:AC-3.Q3
questions.text: Is the level of identity proofing appropriate to the amount of risk associated with the user's access?
questions.supplemental:
Importance: The greater degree of trust associated with a user’s work role, the more important it is to ensure that the individual is who they say they are.

Question Intent: To determine if the organization requires proofs users’ identities appropriate to the level of risk associated with their access.

Individuals in positions of great trust in an organization, particularly those who have access to sensitive information, require a higher level of verification that those whose access is limited. System administrators, for example, might need to verify identity with checks of fingerprints and criminal background investigations. A cook in a cafeteria, however, might not have access to sensitive systems, and so might need to verify identity solely with photo identification and a Social Security number.

Criteria for Full Implementation Response

  • Identity proofing appropriate to a user’s access is performed for all employees and third parties.

Criteria for Partial Implementation Response

  • Identity proofing appropriate to a user’s access is performed for some employees and third parties.
  • (Otherwise, the answer is marked as No Implementation)

Possible evidence

  • Human resources background checks or checklists
  • Lists of contractors or other third parties with access

Reference to standards/source assessments

questions.title: WI:AC-4.Q3
questions.text: Do privileged users employ dedicated privileged accounts to conduct administrative activities?
questions.supplemental:
Importance: Because privileged accounts are of greater use to attackers than typical user accounts, they should not be used for day-to-day computing activities such as reading email or accessing the Internet.

Question Intent: To determine whether the organization limits the use of privileged accounts to solely activities that require the elevated level of access.

Requiring the use of non-privileged accounts when accessing non-security functions limits exposure when operating from within privileged accounts or roles. The inclusion of roles addresses situations where organizations implement access control policies, such as role-based access control, and where a change of role provides the same degree of assurance in the change of access authorizations for the user and the processes acting on behalf of the user as would be provided by a change between a privileged and non-privileged account.

– NIST 800-53 Rev. 5: AC-6 (2)

Criteria for Full Implementation Response

  • Privileged users employ dedicated privileged accounts only when conducting activities that require the heightened level of access.

Criteria for Partial Implementation Response

  • Partial implementation of this control is not allowed.
  • (Otherwise, the answer is marked as No Implementation)

Possible evidence

  • User inventory
  • Identity and Access Management solution user records
  • Employee lists
  • Lists of contractors or other third parties with access

Reference to standards/source assessments

questions.title: WI:IP-3.Q3
questions.text: Does the change management process include an evaluation of potential resilience impacts of the proposed change?
questions.supplemental:
Importance: Determining whether to make a change to a system should be rooted in an understanding of the risks associated with both making and not making the change.

Question Intent: To determine if resilience requirements are evaluated as a result of changes to assets.

The organization should evaluate the impact of asset changes on existing resilience requirements.

The requirements from all the services supported by the changed asset should be considered. Evaluating resilience requirements is especially critical when assets are shared between services.

Criteria for Full Implementation Response

  • The organization evaluates all of the resilience requirements of each asset that supports the critical service when changes to the asset occur.

Criteria for Partial Implementation Response

  • The organization evaluates some of the resilience requirements of each asset that supports the critical service when changes to the asset occur.
  • Or, The organization evaluates all of the resilience requirements of some assets when changes to the asset occur
  • (Otherwise, the answer is marked as No Implementation)

Possible evidence

  • Documented criteria that establishes when a change in requirements must be evaluated
  • Requirements change history with rationale for performing the change
  • Requirements baseline
  • Resilience requirements included in change requests
  • Updated asset resilience requirements

The organization should provide oversight, such as audits or spot-check inspections to ensure that the approved methods of information disposal are being followed.

  • Definition of any key words with examples
  • Qualities of key idea being sought with examples

questions.title: WI:IP-7.Q3
questions.text: Does the organization periodically (but not less than annually) review its cybersecurity policies and procedures to ensure they are producing the intended results?
questions.supplemental:
Importance: Policies and procedures help to ensure consistent, accurate, and repeatable operations. Attackers can exploit improper procedures to gain access to systems or evade detection.

Question Intent: To ensure cybersecurity policies and procedures remain effective and produce intended results by periodic review and measurement.

  • Periodic (as defined by the organization) reviews are needed to ensure that:
  • Policies and procedures reflect current system components
  • Policies take into account the current threat environment and the organization’s risk tolerance
  • Procedures, when performed accurately, meet policy goals
  • Risks related to deficient policies and procedures are identified
  • Actions required to remediate any deficiencies are identified

Criteria for Full Implementation Response

  • All cybersecurity policies and procedures are reviewed periodically (at least annually) and evaluated.

Criteria for Partial Implementation Response

  • The organization has not established a frequency for review.
  • Or, review addresses some, but not all cybersecurity policies and procedures.
  • Or, cybersecurity policies and procedures are reviewed but not evaluated or measured.
  • (Otherwise, the answer is marked as No Implementation)

Possible evidence

  • Document management documentation illustrating regular review
  • Change management records that indicate updates to policies and procedures based on review process

questions.title: WI:IP-9.Q3
questions.text: The organization has a defined continuity of operations plan or business continuity plan, which (at a minimum) contains: (Select one)
questions.supplemental:
Importance: Formal continuity of operations/business continuity planning is necessary to ensure that the critical service can continue to be delivered in the face of adverse circumstances.

Question Intent: To determine if the organization has a documented continuity plan.

  • The plan should address the identification, analysis, and response to a continuity incident.
  • An incident is one or more occurrences that affect organizational assets and have the potential to disrupt operations.
  • An incident significantly impacts the mission critical service and requires the organization to respond to prevent or limit impact to the critical service and the organization.
  • An incident may result from an event or a series of events that requires a response that is beyond standard operating procedures for managing events.
  • An effective continuity capability includes coordination among many organizational entities (e.g., mission or business owners, system owners, authorizing officials, human resources offices, physical security offices, personnel security offices, legal departments, risk executive [function], operations personnel, procurement offices).
  • The organization must plan for how it will:
  • Identify events and incidents
  • Analyze these events and incidents and determine an appropriate response
  • Develop incident declaration criteria
  • Respond to incidents
  • Communicate incident information to stakeholders
  • Staff the plan to meet plan objectives
  • Structure the incident management staff (including roles and responsibilities)
  • Train staff to identify, analyze, and respond to incidents

Criteria for Full Implementation Response

  • There is a documented continuity of operations plan or business continuity plan.

Criteria for Partial Implementation Response

  • The organization has documented some procedures and roles, but lacks a comprehensive plan.
  • (Otherwise, the answer is marked as No Implementation)

Possible evidence

  • Continuity of operations plan
  • Business continuity plan

Reference to standards/source assessments

  • Cyber IST: Q.25.1

  • The tests results should provide information about the organization’s level of preparedness.

questions.title: WI:MA-1.Q3
questions.text: Is the maintenance and repair of assets performed with approved and controlled tools and/or methods?
questions.supplemental:
Importance: Approving, controlling, monitoring, and reviewing maintenance tools address security-related issues associated with maintenance tools that are not within system authorization boundaries and are used specifically for diagnostic and repair actions on organizational systems associated assets.

Question Intent: To determine if the maintenance and repair of critical service/HVA system assets are performed with approved and controlled tools and/or methods.

  • Organizations should approve, control, and monitor information system maintenance tools
  • Organizations have flexibility in determining roles for the approval of maintenance tools and how that approval is documented.
  • Maintenance tools can include hardware, software, and firmware items and may be pre-installed, brought in with maintenance personnel on media, cloud-based, or downloaded from a website. Such tools can be vehicles for transporting malicious code, either intentionally or unintentionally, into a facility and subsequently into systems.
  • Maintenance tools can include hardware and software diagnostic test equipment and packet sniffers.
  • The hardware and software components that support maintenance and are a part of the system (including the software implementing utilities such as “ping,” “ls,” “ipconfig,” or the hardware and software implementing the monitoring port of an Ethernet switch) are not addressed by maintenance tools.
  • A periodic review of maintenance tools facilitates the withdrawal of approval for outdated, unsupported, irrelevant, or no-longer-used tools.
  • Inspect the maintenance tools used by maintenance personnel for improper or unauthorized modifications.
  • Check media containing diagnostic and test programs for malicious code before the media are used in the system
  • Prevent the removal of maintenance equipment containing organizational information
  • Restrict the use of maintenance tools to authorized personnel only.
  • Inspect maintenance tools to ensure the latest software updates and patches are installed

Criteria for Full Implementation Response

  • The maintenance and repair of all assets that support the critical service/HVA environment are performed with approved and controlled tools and/or methods.

Criteria for Partial Implementation Response

  • The maintenance and repair of some assets that support the critical service/HVA environment are performed with approved and controlled tools and/or methods.

Possible evidence

  • A documented list or lists of approved current maintenance tools used to provide maintenance to all assets that support the critical service/HVA environment.

questions.title: WI:NP-1.Q3
questions.text: Do organizational systems generate a unique session identifier for each session with organization-defined randomness requirements and recognize only session identifiers that are system-generated?
questions.supplemental:
Importance: Employing thin clients or similar technology with minimal functionality may reduce the exposure of information, systems, and services to attacks.

Question Intent: To determine if the organization implements organization-defined system components with minimal functionality to help reduce the exposure of the critical service/HVA information systems and services to attack.

  • The deployment of system components with minimal functionality reduces the need to secure every endpoint and may reduce the exposure of information, systems, and services to attacks.
  • Reduced or minimal functionality includes diskless nodes and thin client technologies.

Criteria for Full Implementation Response

  • The organization has implemented system components with minimal functionality and storage for all organization-defined system components that support the critical service/HVA.

Criteria for Partial Implementation Response

  • The organization has implemented system components with minimal functionality and storage for some organization-defined system components that support the critical service/HVA.

Possible evidence

  • Documentation detailing the implementation and configuration system components with minimal functionality and storage that support the critical service/HVA environment.

Reference to standards/source assessments

  • 800-53 SC-25
